content.transcript: Hello, Sarah? You won't believe what happened. I went shopping, and when I got back, the living room was completely different! The children said they wanted to surprise me. First, they had moved the big bookcase from against the wall and put it right in front of the window! I can't see the garden now. And the TV... they had moved it to the other corner, next to the door. But the strangest thing is the table lamp. They had put the table lamp on top of the TV! I don't know what they were thinking. At least they had put the rug in the middle of the floor, which looks nice.

activities.title: What is a Headline?

options.text: To tell the whole story in one sentence.
options.feedback: Headlines are too short to tell the whole story.

options.text: To attract the reader's attention and give an idea of the story.
options.feedback: Correct! Headlines are designed to be catchy and informative.

options.text: To hide the main point of the story.
options.feedback: The goal is to summarize, not to hide information.

options.text: To use as many words as possible.
options.feedback: Headlines are usually very short.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a newspaper headline?
questions.explanation: Headlines grab your attention and quickly tell you what the news article is about.

options.text: They are always written as long, complete sentences.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Headlines often leave out words like 'is', 'are', 'a', 'the'.

options.text: They are printed in a very small font.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Headlines use large, bold fonts to stand out.

options.text: They are often not complete sentences.
options.feedback: Correct! To save space and be more dramatic, headlines often omit small words.

options.text: They are always written in the past tense.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Headlines can use different tenses, often the present simple for recent events.

questions.question: Which of these is a typical feature of a newspaper headline?
questions.explanation: To be short and impactful, headlines often leave out articles (a, the) and auxiliary verbs (is, are, was, were).

activities.title: Fisherman Escapes Drowning

content.passage: A brave helicopter pilot nearly flew into the sea in Mukalla Bay yesterday when saving the life of a lone fisherman. ‘The wheels of the helicopter were almost in the water,’ said Captain Mansour of the National Coastguard, ‘but the boat was sinking. It was the only thing I could do.’ His partner, Sergeant Rashid, threw a life-belt into the sea and helped the fisherman climb into the helicopter. A few minutes later the boat sank. Jim Duffy, who lives and works in Mukalla, said that he was very lucky. He had nearly drowned. ‘I’ll never go fishing alone again,’ he added.

content.transcript: Rashid: The sea looks a bit rough today, Captain. Captain: Yes, it does, doesn't it? I think a wind is blowing up, Rashid. Captain: Well, five minutes more and we'll ... Rashid: Hey, Captain, look! Quick! Over there! I think there's something in the water. Captain: Where? I can't see anything. Rashid: Almost straight ahead. About two kilometres. Captain: Yes. I can see it now. It looks like ... yes ... definitely ... we've got somebody in trouble. Here we go. Captain: How many people can you see, Rashid? Rashid: One. He's alone. But he's sinking. We've got to get to him quickly. Captain: We're going down. Get out that life-belt. Rashid: Look out, Captain, we're nearly in the water. If we go any closer ... Captain: Go on. I can hold it here. Grab him. Rashid: I've got him, Captain. Captain: Right, let's get out of here.

options.text: The Minister said the new road is a great success.
options.feedback: Not quite. When the reporting verb ('said') is in the past, the verb in the reported clause usually changes tense.

options.feedback: Excellent! The verb 'is' changes to 'was' in reported speech.

options.text: The Minister says that the new road was a great success.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The reporting verb in the original sentence is 'said' (past tense), not 'says' (present tense).

questions.question: Direct speech: The Minister said, "The new road is a great success."
questions.explanation: In reported speech, if the reporting verb (e.g., said, told) is in the past tense, the verb tense in the reported clause 'backshifts'. Present simple ('is') becomes past simple ('was').

options.text: He added that this saved a lot of time.
options.feedback: Correct! 'saves' (present simple) changes to 'saved' (past simple).

options.text: He added that this saves a lot of time.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Remember to change the tense of the verb after a past tense reporting verb.

options.text: He adds that this saved a lot of time.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The reporting verb should remain in the past tense ('added').

questions.question: Direct speech: He added, "This saves a lot of time."
questions.explanation: The present simple verb 'saves' changes to the past simple 'saved' when the reporting verb 'added' is in the past.

content.transcript: Dear Fred, Well, we finally arrived after a horrible flight. It was terrible. I thought that I was going to die. We're staying at a horrible little hotel. It's called 'La Vista' and it's about three kilometres from the beach. Our room is nothing to write home about. It's much too small for the wife and me and it's above an all-night restaurant. Which reminds me, the food here is awful. I haven't had a good cheese sandwich for a week. And the people! They never stop talking. Boring, boring, boring. And on top of that, we've visited hundreds of boring castles. I can't wait to get home. I hope that you are looking after my pigeons. Cheers, Bill

Our room is very small, but then, you can't have everything, can you? The food is delicious and I can get a lovely cup of tea. And the people in the hotel are ever so nice. Very friendly. Just like at home. We've visited lots of interesting places and we're having a lovely time. I can't wait to come back next year. I hope that you and your family are well. Love, Betty

content.transcript: Wife: Let's go out this afternoon. Husband: Must we? I'd rather stay in and watch TV. Wife: Oh! I wanted to see that exhibition of paintings by local artists. Husband: Well, you can. Ask your sister if she wants to go. It's Ladies afternoon, isn't it? Wife: Oh, yes, so it is. Mmm! No, I don't think I'll bother. All right then. What's on TV? Husband: There's a programme about poets at 6. Should be good. Wife: No, thank you. That doesn't interest me. Not one bit. Husband: Oh! Well, there's something interesting later. It's called 'There's only one Earth'. Wife: What's it about? Husband: It's about animals. Animals in danger. Wife: Oh, no! I don't like programmes like that. They make me sad. I'd rather watch something cheerful. Something that'll make me laugh. Husband: Well, there's 'Marhabah' at eight o'clock. No, no, wait a minute. You like answering questions, don't you? Wife: Answering questions? What do you mean, answering questions? Husband: Oh - you know! Questions on history, geography, who did what? When? That sort of thing. Wife: I see. Yes, I like answering questions. Husband: Good. Now I know which programme you'll want to watch.

activities.title: Reading: Letters to the Newspaper

content.passage:
## PUBLIC OPINION

**Dear Sir,**

I totally agree with your report last week called *Things were better then*. Things were better then. For example, life was quieter thirty years ago. There was no noise from air conditioners, fast cars and jet planes. I also agree with you about TV. In my opinion, we do not need it. When I was younger, we heard all the latest news and stories from our friends. Now people sit by themselves in front of their television sets. You are also right about food. I believe that fresh fish from the sea is better than fish from the fridge. I miss the old days.

Yours,

Yousif Saleh

---

**Dear Sir,**

I cannot agree with the person who wrote *Things were better then. Things are better now*. First, TV. In my opinion, we need it. I think that TV teaches us a lot. My children, for example, watch the international news and other programmes about other countries. They know more than I do. I think that the writer is also wrong about food. It is true that we had fresh fish. We still do. And what about all the other fresh food that we can get now? When did your writer last go to the market? Finally, I totally disagree with him about the new roads. Thirty years ago journeys could take days. Now we can drive anywhere in the country in a few hours. I think that your writer has forgotten how difficult life was.

Yours,

Khalil Ahmed

content.passage:
A reporter asked people: 'Young people today are lazy and selfish. They don't care about anybody except themselves. What do you think?'

**1ST PASSER-BY**
What! Lazy and selfish? It's not true. I'm not lazy. My friends are not lazy. We want work, but we can't get jobs. I've answered eighty-nine advertisements for jobs but I still haven't got one. The truth is that the older generation don't care about us. That's my opinion. Take it or leave it.

**2ND PASSER-BY**
Yes. I agree with you totally. Young people are lazy and selfish. There are plenty of jobs if they want them. The truth is that they don't want to work. They just want to have a good time.

**3RD PASSER-BY**
Oh no! I don't agree. You're wrong. I know a lot of young people and they are all kind and very helpful. Some young people come to my house and help me all the time. They do my shopping and work in my garden. In my opinion, young people are wonderful.

**4TH PASSER-BY**
There isn't an easy answer to that. All young people are not the same. Some are lazy and some are not. Some don't care about anything and some care a lot. It's the same with middle-aged people and older people.

content.transcript:
1st Passer-by: What! Lazy and selfish? It's not true. I'm not lazy. My friends are not lazy. We want work, but we can't get jobs. I've answered eighty-nine advertisements for jobs but I still haven't got one. The truth is that the older generation don't care about us. That's my opinion. Take it or leave it.
2nd Passer-by: Yes. I agree with you totally. Young people are lazy and selfish. There are plenty of jobs if they want them. The truth is that they don't want to work. They just want to have a good time.
3rd Passer-by: Oh no! I don't agree. You're wrong. I know a lot of young people and they are all kind and very helpful. Some young people come to my house and help me all the time. They do my shopping and work in my garden. In my opinion, young people are wonderful.
4th Passer-by: There isn't an easy answer to that. All young people are not the same. Some are lazy and some are not. Some don't care about anything and some care a lot. It's the same with middle-aged people and older people.

activities.compensates: WB4.11A listening activity with cassette.
activities.instruction: Listen to four people giving their opinion on the statement: 'Young people today are lazy and selfish'. Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for if each person agrees, disagrees, or half-agrees.

activities.title: Reading: Success at Last

content.passage:
The sharks moved slowly round the boat in big circles. We sat and waited. I looked at Mansour. He was looking anxiously at the sky. ‘Shamal’, he said. ‘Not another one,’ I thought, but he was right. The sky darkened until it was almost black. The sea now looked grey and dangerous and our boat began to bob up and down on the water. Then the wind hit us.

The next fourteen hours were the longest hours of my life. The wind howled around us. We could not hear each other even when we shouted. Huge mountains of water crashed heavily down on the boat. It began to fill up, so we grabbed anything that would hold water. We bailed for our lives hour after hour. At about two in the morning the wind began to drop.

The sun felt warm on my face. I opened my eyes sleepily. Mansour was making coffee. The sea was quiet. The waves had gone. The sharks had gone too. I asked Mansour when we could dive. He said that we would have to wait for seven or eight hours. He was right again.

We dived early in the afternoon. The water was still a little sandy, but we could see where we were going. As we swam up to the wreck, I could see that things had changed. Now I could see the whole ship. It was no longer half buried in sand and mud.

Mansour pointed to the middle of the ship. We swam down and in, into a treasure room. The colours had not changed in two thousand years. Beautiful gold and silver jewellery with rich green and blue stones lay everywhere. There were beautifully painted jars as well, some broken, but still whole.

What activity does Bob suggest for enjoying the scenery in Scotland?
Which two activities can be done in Norfolk, according to Bob?
In the end, where does Bob recommend Ahmed go fishing?

content.transcript:
Presenter: Ahmed Said is staying with Bob Farmer and his family. Bob is asking Ahmed what he wants to do and see in the UK.
Ahmed: Well, there are lots of things I want to do. I don't know where to begin.
Bob: Why not do something you haven't done before?
Ahmed: Well, I'd like to go climbing.
Bob: Climbing? Then you should go to the Lake District. It's very beautiful there and it's got the highest mountains in England.
Ahmed: Scotland is very beautiful too, I believe.
Bob: Yes, it is, very.
Ahmed: Can we go there?
Bob: Of course. But if you want to enjoy the scenery, why not go camping? It's more exciting than staying in a hotel.
Ahmed: That's a good idea. I like camping.
Bob: And when you're in Scotland, you should go shopping in Edinburgh. You can buy things there you won't find anywhere else.
Ahmed: OK. That sounds fine. And I want to go sailing.
Bob: Hm. You should go to Norfolk for that.
Ahmed: And fishing?
Bob: Yes, you can go fishing in Norfolk too. But, wait a minute, you'll have seen parts of England and Scotland. So why not go fishing in Wales? It's very pleasant there.
Ahmed: Fine. That suits me. So where should we go first?

activities.title: The White Family's Holiday

content.passage:
Marrakesh was our first stop. Anne and her father drove into the Atlas mountains. She took her climbing boots and Sam took his fishing rod. Peter and I wandered round the beautiful old city. In the evening we all sat in the Djemma El Fna Square. All around us were musicians, dancers and story tellers. Above us was the famous minaret of the magnificent Koutoubia mosque.
Our next stop was Casablanca. Anne and I lay on the beach in the sun. Peter spent the whole day in or on the water. Sam spent the day fishing.
Last stop was Tangier. We visited the tomb of Ibn Battuta, but we spent most of our time in the souks. Beautiful pottery, magnificent gold and silver jewellery, superb leather jackets and skirts, lovely cotton and silk kaftans - the choice was endless, but, unfortunately, our money was not. It was time to leave Morocco.

activities.title: Planning a Holiday

questions.question: What does Mrs. White's husband love to do?
What is the daughter, Anne, interested in?
What does the son, Peter, like?
What is the one thing the whole family agrees on?

content.transcript: Every year, we have the same problem in our family. The question comes up - where shall we go on holiday? And there isn't an easy answer to that question. You see, we're all different. My husband loves fishing, so he has to be near a river, a lake, the sea - anywhere he can go fishing. My daughter, Anne, likes mountain climbing. Mountain climbing! I don't understand it, but that's all she's interested in. Then there's my son, Peter. He has to be near the sea. He likes all sorts of water sports - swimming, sailing, water skiing, wind surfing - water sports of any kind. And me? I'm interested in the past. I love ancient ruins, old buildings, museums, anything that tells me about the past. So you see, we're all different. But there is one thing we agree on. We all like the sun. So we need a country where there's lots and lots of sunshine. And I think we've found the answer to our question. This year we're going to Morocco. It looks great. I think it's got something for everybody.

activities.title: Highlights of Yemen

content.passage:
Yemen is a wonderful place for a holiday. It has something for everyone. 

**A Shibam:** This town is famous for its tall houses, built of mud. Some have 8 floors and a few are over 500 years old. 

**B Aden:** Here tourists should visit the National Museum where they can see superb exhibits of ancient Arabian cultures. You can also enjoy local fish, caught daily, in Aden's excellent fish restaurants. 

**C Wadi Dahr:** The magnificent Palace on the Rock was built in the 1930s. There are wells inside, dug through the rock. 

**D Jibla:** Some say this is the most beautiful town in Yemen. The Great Mosque here was built in 1088 by Queen Arwa, who ruled the Sulayhid State for 50 years. 

**E Sana'a:** Sana'a is the capital of Yemen. The old walled city contains a fascinating collection of ancient souks, mosques and traditional houses. 

**F The sea off Sirah Island:** One of Yemen's greatest attractions is its beautiful coast.

content.passage:
A 7-Day Trip to Yemen for a First-Time Visitor

**Day 1-2: Sana'a**
Arrive at Sana'a International Airport. Check into a traditional guesthouse in the Old City. Spend two days exploring the UNESCO World Heritage site, visiting the Great Mosque and shopping in the Souq al-Milh.

**Day 3-5: Socotra Island**
Take a flight to Socotra. We will spend three days exploring this unique island. You will see the famous Dragon's Blood Trees and enjoy the beautiful beaches. Accommodation will be eco-camps.

**Day 6: Shibam Hadramawt**
Fly back to the mainland and travel to Shibam, known as the 'Manhattan of the Desert'. We will explore the ancient mud-brick skyscrapers and learn about the city's history.

**Day 7: Departure**
Return to Sana'a for your departure flight.

activities.title: Reading: Famous Explorers

content.passage:
Throughout history, extraordinary men have set off into the unknown to find new countries. Some went with the hope of making lots of money; others were ordered by their rulers to find new colonies for their countries; others just wanted to find out more about the world. All of them were extremely brave.

Sinbad of the Sea or Sinbad the Sailor is one of the earliest of these. Of course, he was not a real person but a fictional character in old stories. However, there is no doubt that the stories of his travels are based on actual voyages made by Arab seamen of the 8th and 9th centuries. They were the leading navigators of the time, using detailed knowledge of the stars to find their way. Showing great bravery and faith, they sailed around India and set up trading links with China nearly 12,000 kilometres from their home ports.

Christopher Columbus (1451 - 1506, Genoa) was sure it was possible to sail west to the Indies across the vast Atlantic Ocean. He got money for his voyage from the queen of Spain and he and his men left the port of Palos in August, 1492. He reached land 70 days later and claimed the land for Spain. He had discovered a new continent - America. However, Columbus thought he had arrived in the Indies, so he called the native people 'the Indians'.

Amerigo Vespucci (1451 - 1512, Florence), a merchant, was the first European to see South America. Because he had discovered a new continent, a new map was needed. The man who made the map named the continent 'America' after its discoverer.

Vasco da Gama (1460-1524, Portugal) in 1497 became the first man to sail to India from Europe round the southern tip of Africa. He reached the Portuguese colony of Goa. In the last part of his journey, he made use of information provided by Ahmed Ibn Majid, the famous navigator from the Arabian Gulf.

Ibn Battuta (1304 - 1378, Morocco) wanted to travel all over the world. In 1325 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca. He continued travelling through Turkey, up the River Volga, south to northern India, and in 1344 he reached China. His other journeys he explored East and West Africa and Spain. He came back home in 1353 to write about his travels.

Abel Tasman (1603 - 1659, Holland) discovered New Zealand in 1643 and named it after a part of Holland. He also discovered an island off the southern coast of Australia, which was later named Tasmania after him.

James Cook (1728 - 1779, Britain) was a Captain in the British Navy. He explored the islands of the South Pacific Ocean, made detailed maps of Australia and New Zealand, and was the first European to sail to the Antarctic. He was killed in a fight on the island of Hawaii.

Roald Amundsen (1872 - 1928, Norway) was a professional explorer. He was the first man to sail to Alaska through the North West Passage and also won the race to the South Pole in 1911. He disappeared in 1928 during a rescue mission in the Arctic.

content.transcript: Marco Polo was a merchant and explorer from Venice, Italy, born in 1254. Along with his father and uncle, he embarked on an epic journey to Asia. They travelled along the Silk Road and reached China, where he spent 17 years in the service of the emperor Kublai Khan. He saw many incredible inventions there, such as paper money and eyeglasses, which were unknown in Europe at the time. After returning to Venice, he was captured during a war and put in prison. While in prison, he dictated the story of his travels to a fellow inmate. The resulting book, 'The Travels of Marco Polo', inspired future generations of explorers, including Christopher Columbus.

activities.title: How Fit Are You?

content.passage:
A lot of people play games to stay fit. But you can also do exercises. Here are three. Do them to find out if you are fit.

### Exercise 1
Walk up and down some steps (about fifteen) three times. Are you out of breath? Or can you breathe easily? Can you talk to somebody without difficulty?

### Exercise 2
Run on the spot. This means that you run but stay in the same place. Lift your feet at least fifteen centimetres from the floor. Do this for three minutes. Can you do this easily?

### Exercise 3
Get a chair. Step on and off it quite quickly, starting first with your right foot then with your left foot. Do this for three minutes. Are you tired and out of breath?

questions.explanation: Ed Farmer says, 'Smoking made me feel big too. Made me feel older and more clever.'

content.transcript: Presenter: Yesterday Tony Newton spoke to some people at Dr King's clinic. Listen and make notes. Tony: First I spoke to Mr John Ross. Mr Ross is thirty-seven years old. He's a driver from North London. Mr Ross, you went to Dr King's clinic? Mr Ross: Yes, that's right, I did. It was very helpful. Those films were - oh, and the talks as well - they were very good. Tony: And did you stop smoking? Mr Ross: Yes - for a while. And I felt much better. No coughs. I felt very fit. But, I'm afraid, I started again. Last week. Tony: You're smoking again. You haven't stopped. So the clinic didn't help you. Mr Ross: Well, it did a lot. I used to smoke on average sixty cigarettes a day. Now I only smoke ten. So I smoke less. But I'd still like to give it up completely. Tony: Next I spoke to Mrs Meg Ward. Mrs Ward, do you mind if I ask how old you are? Mrs Ward: No, not at all. I'm twenty-six. Tony: And what do you do? Mrs Ward: I'm a nurse. Tony: And has the clinic helped you? Mrs Ward: Oh, yes. It was fantastic. I gave up smoking three months ago. I haven't smoked a cigarette since then. Tony: Were you a heavy smoker? Mrs Ward: Quite heavy. I used to smoke about twenty-five a day. Tony: Will you start again? Mrs Ward: Definitely not. It was hard to stop, but I have. I won't start again. Tony: And finally I spoke to Ed Farmer, an eighteen-year-old student. Ed, you used to be a heavy smoker, didn't you? Ed Farmer: Oh, yeah. Forty a day. I used to smoke all the time at home and in school. Tony: Were you allowed to smoke in school? Ed Farmer: No, they wouldn't allow that. I just never got caught. Tony: Forty a day! That's a lot for an eighteen-year-old. Ed Farmer: Well, I started when I was eleven. The big boys used to smoke a lot. Smoking made me feel big too. Made me feel older and more clever. Tony: And how did the clinic help you? Ed Farmer: Talking to other people there helped. Everybody was trying to stop smoking. So I decided to try too. And it worked. I've stopped now and I don't ever want to start again. Smoking isn't clever. It's stupid.

content.transcript: Presenter: Today, I'm talking to Dr Susan King. Dr King, you run a clinic for smokers. Who comes to your clinic? Dr King: All kinds of people. Young people, old people. Men and women. Presenter: And can you help them? Dr King: Oh, yes. We can help them a lot. But they have to want to stop. We can't make them stop. Presenter: Is it very difficult? Dr King: Yes, it is. People who are addicted to smoking find it very difficult to stop. But it isn't impossible. Presenter: And it is very dangerous, isn't it? Dr King: Yes, it is. Very dangerous. More people are killed by smoking than on the roads. Presenter: Really? Dr King: Yes. Smoking makes your heart beat faster, and it can cause cancer. Presenter: Thank you, Dr King. activities.title: Understanding the Passive Voice

options.text: When we want to know who did the action.
options.feedback: This is usually when we use the active voice.

options.text: When what is done is more important than who does it.
options.feedback: Correct! The focus is on the action or the object that receives the action.

options.text: When we are talking about the past.
options.feedback: The passive can be used in any tense, not just the past.

questions.question: When do we use the passive voice?
questions.explanation: The passive voice is used to emphasize the action or the result, rather than the person or thing performing the action.

options.feedback: The -ing form is used for continuous tenses.
The base form is used in simple present or with modals in the active voice.
Excellent! Passive sentences always use a form of 'to be' + the past participle (e.g., is built, was taken, has been seen).

questions.question: Which part of the verb is always used in a passive sentence?
questions.explanation: The structure of the passive is always a form of the verb 'to be' followed by the past participle of the main verb.

activities.title: A Doctor's Day

content.passage:
Dr Patel is a general practitioner in London.

**Morning surgery: The first patient**
Dr Patel: Now, Tom. What's the matter with you?
Tom: I've got a pain in my stomach, Doctor. It really hurts.
Dr Patel: Does it hurt all the time?
Tom: No. Only in the mornings.
Dr Patel: Do you eat anything at night? Just before you go to bed?
Tom: Yes. I usually have some chocolates and lemonade.
Dr Patel: Tom, that's what gives you stomach-ache. Don't do it any more. And if you get stomach-ache, take one of these tablets.

**Evening House call: Mrs Rix**
Dr Patel: Good evening, Mrs. Rix. How are you tonight?
Mrs Rix: Worse, Doctor. I had a very bad night last night. I had terrible pains in my legs.
Dr Patel: Are you taking your medicine?
Mrs Rix: Well, I didn't take any yesterday. Or the day before. I felt better.
Dr Patel: Mrs Rix, you must take your medicine. Three spoonfuls a day after meals.

**Evening On the telephone: Mrs Jones**
Mrs Jones: Good evening, Doctor. I'm sorry to phone so late. I've got a temperature of forty degrees and I ache all over.
Dr Patel: I see. It sounds like flu.
Mrs Jones: What should I do?
Dr Patel: Don't worry, Mrs Jones. Keep warm and have plenty to drink. Fruit juice, if you've got it. No milk. I'll come round tomorrow morning after surgery.

activities.title: Why Prevention is Better Than Cure

content.passage:
The old saying, 'Prevention is better than cure,' holds a simple but powerful truth. It means that it is wiser, easier, and cheaper to stop an illness from happening in the first place than to treat it after it has already started. When a person gets sick, they may experience pain, miss school or work, and face expensive medical bills. For a country, widespread illness can put a huge strain on healthcare services. Even if an illness is cured, it might have long-term effects on a person's health. 

There are many simple steps we can take to prevent illness. Good personal hygiene, like washing hands frequently with soap, is one of the most effective methods. A balanced diet, regular exercise, and getting enough sleep are also crucial personal habits that strengthen our bodies. In the home, keeping kitchens clean and storing food properly can prevent food poisoning. By taking these preventative measures, we can lead healthier, happier lives and avoid the difficulties that come with being sick.

activities.title: Reading: Great Names in Medicine

content.passage:
### Ancient knowledge
By the first century AD, Greek scientists and philosophers had amassed and written down on manuscripts a great deal of knowledge from ancient scholars. The famous library of Alexandria, Egypt, was a treasure house of such knowledge. Among these manuscripts was a copy of the work of Hippocrates, the father of medicine. This great library was destroyed by the Romans. The libraries of Rome were in turn destroyed by invaders. The period following the loss of this wealth of knowledge is known in Western history as the 'Dark Ages'. Centuries of learning could have been lost to the world but for Arab scholars who produced Arabic versions of many Greek works.

### Al Rhaze c. 865 - 925
In the 7th century AD, the boundaries of Islam stretched from Spain to India. There were some outstanding Muslim scholars at this time. One of the most famous physicians was Al Rhaze who produced the great work Al-Hawi. In it he recorded Greek, Arab and even some Hindu medical knowledge, as well as his own medical discoveries. In time, Western scholars became interested in Muslim learning and translated Arabic works, including Al-Hawi, into Latin. In this way, knowledge based on long forgotten Greek works was again available in Europe.

### Vesalius, Andreas 1514 - 1564
Vesalius was a Flemish anatomist known as the father of modern anatomy. Until the middle of the 16th century, people believed that the different parts of the human body were controlled by the stars. Vesalius changed all that. He dissected or cut up human bodies and wrote a description of every part.

### Harvey, William 1578 - 1657
Harvey was an English anatomist who discovered the circulation of the blood. One thing that Vesalius did not understand was how the human heart worked. Harvey found the answer. He proved that the heart acts as a pump and that blood is moved around the body. He also discovered that blood moves away from the heart in arteries and back to the heart in veins.

### Jenner, Edward 1749 - 1823
Jenner was a British doctor who developed the first effective vaccine against smallpox, a killer disease at the time. Jenner noticed that people who milked cows got a disease called cowpox. These people did not get smallpox. Jenner put matter from a cowpox sore into a cut on the arm of an eight-year-old boy. Then he infected the boy with smallpox. The boy remained healthy.

### Pasteur, Louis 1822 - 1895
Pasteur was a French chemist who proved that microbes or bacteria lived in the air. They could make milk go sour. More importantly, they could cause disease. He showed that they could be killed by heat. He also showed that they could be weakened, injected into the body and make the person safe from attacks by the full strength bacteria. In this way he explained and developed Jenner's work.

### Lister, Joseph 1827 - 1912
Lister was a British surgeon who pioneered the use of antiseptics in surgery. He realized that bacteria might be the cause of infections in wounds after surgery. Since he could not use heat in surgery, he used carbolic acid instead and became the father of antiseptics.

activities.title: Jobs That Serve the Public

content.passage: Public service jobs are very important for our society. People in these jobs serve the public. For example, a traffic policeman's job is to control traffic. He helps all road users: motorists, cyclists, and pedestrians (people who walk). His job can be difficult because some people do not obey the rules. Another important job is being a fireman. A fireman's job is to put out fires and rescue people. This job is dangerous, and firemen say that if people were more careful, there would be fewer fires. At airports and borders, you will find an immigration officer. His job is to check people's passports to make sure they can enter the country. It is part of our culture and religion to be polite and treat these visitors with respect.

activities.title: Reading for Detail

content.passage:
Interviewer: Welcome, Officer Salma. Thank you for joining us. First, how old are you?
Salma: I'm seventeen.
Interviewer: And you're already a policewoman. That's impressive. Where do you work?
Salma: I work at the airport, in the security department.
Interviewer: Airport security is a very responsible job. Why is it so important?
Salma: It's important because some people try to take dangerous things onto planes. We have to check all the luggage to ensure everyone is safe.
Interviewer: Do you open every bag?
Salma: No, definitely not. We only open luggage that shows something we can't identify on the X-ray screen.
Interviewer: I see. Some of your friends tease you, don't they? They say you are too short to be a policewoman.
Salma: Yes, they do! But I tell them that being a good police officer isn't about being big. It's about being smart and responsible.
Interviewer: That's a great answer. What do you like most about your job?
Salma: I like knowing that my work helps people feel safe. It's a great responsibility.
Interviewer: What are your plans for the future? Will you continue in this role?
Salma: My father suggested I think about my future. I want to continue with my education, and perhaps join the air-wing of the police one day.

activities.title: Grammar Focus: Adjective Order

content.passage:
When we use more than one adjective to describe a noun, we usually put them in a specific order. This helps our sentences sound natural. The general order is:

1.  **Opinion:** What you think about it (e.g., *beautiful, horrible, lovely*)
2.  **Size:** How big or small it is (e.g., *large, small, tiny*)
3.  **Age:** How old it is (e.g., *old, new, fifteen-year-old*)
4.  **Shape:** What shape it is (e.g., *round, square, curly*)
5.  **Colour:** What colour it is (e.g., *blue, black, red*)
6.  **Origin:** Where it is from (e.g., *Scottish, Arabian, Japanese*)
7.  **Material:** What it is made of (e.g., *cotton, silk, gold*)

For example, we say 'a *lovely new silk* dress' (Opinion -> Age -> Material), not 'a silk new lovely dress'. We also say 'a *superb old Islamic* building' (Opinion -> Age -> Origin).

activities.title: The Many Jobs of the Fire Brigade

content.passage:
Most people think the fire brigade only puts out fires, but their job is much bigger than that. Apart from fighting fires, they play a crucial role in public safety. A major part of their work is fire prevention. Firefighters visit schools and businesses to advise people on safety. They point out dangerous things, like blocked exits, and recommend safety equipment such as smoke-alarms and fire extinguishers. They also check that this equipment is working correctly. 

Firefighters also provide vital help in traffic accidents. They are often the first to arrive at the scene. They might need to put out a fire in a car or use special equipment to free people who are trapped inside a damaged vehicle. 

Finally, the fire brigade handles many unexpected jobs. These can range from rescuing animals stuck in high places to helping people who are trapped in elevators. Their work is varied and essential for the community's well-being.

content.transcript: In case of a fire, your safety is the top priority. First, stay calm. If you see a lot of smoke, get down on the floor and crawl. The air is cleaner near the ground. Cover your mouth and nose with a wet cloth if possible to avoid breathing in smoke. If the fire is very small, you can try to use a fire extinguisher. But if the fire is big, do not try to fight it. Your main goal is to get out of the building safely. Once you are outside, call the fire brigade immediately. Do not go back inside for any reason.

content.passage:
## Salah School Blaze: Caretaker Hailed as Hero

A huge fire completely destroyed the main building of Salah Secondary School last night. The blaze, which started around 10 PM, was blazing out of control by the time fire-engines arrived. Officials later said that an electrical fault was to blame for the incident.

The school's caretaker, Mr. Ahmed, was hailed as a hero. He saw the smoke and immediately rushed to the scene. He used a small hose to fight the fire before it spread to the new science labs. Although two firefighters were slightly injured while fighting the blaze, no one else was harmed thanks to Mr. Ahmed's quick actions. The headteacher said, 'He is a true hero. He saved an important part of our school.'

content.passage:
### Article 1: The Daily News

**Fire at City Warehouse**

A large fire destroyed the old city warehouse on Market Street last night. The fire started at around 10 p.m. Firefighters arrived quickly and fought the blaze for over four hours. By 2 a.m., the fire was under control. The building was empty at the time of the fire, and no one was seriously hurt. The police are investigating the incident.

### Article 2: The Evening Post

**Market Street Blaze Investigated**

The old warehouse on Market Street was completely destroyed by a fire last night. The fire, which started at 10 p.m., burned for four hours before firefighters could control it. One firefighter, Ali Hassan, was injured when a part of the roof fell while he was checking the building. He was taken to hospital but was released this morning. Investigators believe the fire had started because of old electrical equipment that overheated. The warehouse had been empty for five years before the fire.

content.transcript:
Presenter: A fishing boat is missing. Nobody knows where it is. The boat, with three fishermen in it, left Shuqrah yesterday morning. The boat did not return to Shuqrah yesterday evening. The people in the village were worried. They called the police. Now the police are looking for the missing boat. Here is part of a conversation between a police boat and Police Headquarters.
HQ: Calling Boat 7. Calling Boat 7. Come in, Boat 7. Over!
Boat: Boat 7 here. Boat 7 here. Over!
HQ: Have you seen anything yet? Over!
Boat: No. Nothing. We haven't seen anything. Over!
HQ: What is your position? Where are you now? Over!
Boat: We're about 20 kilometres south of Zinjibar. Over!
HQ: What's the weather like? What's the weather like? Over!
Boat: It's bad. Quite bad. And it's getting worse. There's a strong wind blowing from the north east. Over!
HQ: Can we do anything? Can we help? Over!
Boat: Yes. Yes, you can. A helicopter would help. Repeat. A helicopter. It'll be dark in two hours. We must find that fishing boat before then. We've got to. Over!
HQ: OK. We'll call...

activities.title: Laws for Young People in the UK

content.passage: In the United Kingdom, many laws affect young people and change as they get older. These laws say what you must, must not, or may do. For example, school is compulsory from the age of 5. At this age, a child must also pay a fare on public transport. At 16, you can leave school and start a full-time job. Joining the armed forces is also possible at 16, but it requires parental consent. However, you cannot vote in an election until you are 18. The law also forbids people under 18 from buying a shotgun, and a special licence is required for adults who wish to own one.

activities.title: Making Questions Polite

correct: Do you know where I can buy a spade?
sentences.original: Where can I buy a spade?
sentences.explanation: The word order in the main part of the question stays the same because 'can' is a modal verb.

correct: Can you tell me how far the bus station is?
sentences.original: How far is the bus station?
sentences.explanation: The verb 'is' moves to the end, after the subject 'the bus station'.

correct: Do you know what time the bookshop opens?
sentences.original: What time does the bookshop open?
sentences.explanation: We remove the auxiliary verb 'does' and add 's' to the main verb 'open'.

correct: Do you know what Faisal’s telephone number is?
sentences.original: What is Faisal’s telephone number?
sentences.explanation: The verb 'is' moves to the end, after the subject 'Faisal's telephone number'.

activities.compensates: Workbook activity 1.3C, providing instant feedback.
activities.instruction: Change the direct questions into polite, indirect questions using the phrase provided. This is the same as Workbook page 4, exercise C.

activities.title: A Guide to Staying Healthy

content.passage: To keep healthy, it is important to follow some basic rules. First, a balanced diet is essential. This means eating a variety of foods, including fruits which are full of vitamins, and avoiding too many fats. Second, regular exercise helps keep your body fit and strong. Third, good hygiene can prevent the spread of diseases. For example, cleaning a small injury with disinfectant can stop an infection from developing. For more serious illnesses like the flu, rest is important. Sometimes, a doctor might give you a prescription for tablets to help you recover. Finally, prevention is key. For diseases like cholera, it is crucial to be immunized, especially when traveling. Following this advice can help you avoid getting sick and needing a doctor.

activities.title: Read the Story: Barry Jones - London schoolboy

content.passage:
'Come on, Sue. Give me the cornflakes. I'm late.'
'Say please,' said Sue, giggling.
'Please,' I said. 'And hurry up! It's half past eight!'
'Dad can take you in his taxi,' said Sue.
'No, he can't. He's gone,' I said.
'Do you want an egg, dear?' shouted Mum from the kitchen.
'No thanks, Mum. I'm late.'
Sue giggled again and I wanted to know why.
'What are you laughing at?'
'Nothing,' said Sue and giggled for the third time.
Sue was just thirteen, about two years younger than me, and sometimes I could not understand her.

Ten minutes later, I was sitting upstairs on the bus with my Geography textbook open on my knee. There was a test in the first period.
'Hi, Barry,' somebody said behind me. It was my friend, Kevin. We had been at Central Comprehensive School for almost five years. I turned round and Kevin laughed. 'Your face!' he said. 'It's all black. Don't you wash?'
'Sue!' I shouted. She had put some trick soap in the bathroom before I went in. My face had got dirtier instead of cleaner.

The bus stopped. We flew downstairs and I ran to the school washroom. Then I ran to the Geography lesson.
'I'm sorry I'm late, sir,' I panted.
'I'm sorry too,' said Mr Edwards, our Geography teacher. 'Sit down and do the test.'

'Where's that soap, Sue?' I asked when I got home. She didn't answer.
'Anne's coming,' she said.
'Who's Anne?' I asked.
'She's my pen-friend from France,' said Sue. 'She's coming to stay next week - for a month.'

activities.title: Conditional Sentences

content.passage:
Type 1 Conditionals:
When a condition is likely to be fulfilled, the result is likely to happen.
Structure: If + present simple, ... will + verb
Example: If I work hard, I will pass the exam.

Type 2 Conditionals:
When a condition is not likely or impossible, the result is not likely to happen.
Structure: If + past simple, ... would + verb
Example: If I had a helicopter, I would fly over the mountains.

content.passage:
Issa Said, Traffic Policeman: My job is to make roads safe for all road users. Most motorists obey the rules of the road. But some do stupid things and this makes them a danger to themselves and others. Cyclists and pedestrians can be silly too. If everybody obeyed the rules, our roads would be much safer.

Ali Abdullah, Immigration Officer: I work at the airport. My job is to check people entering and leaving the country by examining their passports. First-time visitors sometimes have problems with the regulations. I try to help them as much as I can. I am always polite and treat every person with respect.

Salman Nasser, Helicopter Pilot: I'm in the air-wing of the police. My job is to help people in trouble, for example, someone who is very ill in a place where an ambulance can't go. Helicopters can go almost anywhere very quickly, so I am sometimes able to save lives.

Fuad Rashid, Fireman: My job is to put out fires. My job is dangerous because fires can be extremely dangerous. Some accidents happen because people are careless. If people were more careful, there would be fewer fires.

content.transcript: My name is Salman Nasser and I'm in the air-wing of the police. I'm a helicopter pilot. My job is to help people in trouble. For example, someone may be very ill. He may be a long way from a hospital in a place where a car or ambulance can't get to him. Helicopters can go almost anywhere and they can get there very quickly. So I am sometimes able to save lives. If things like these didn't happen, I'd be out of a job - a job that I love.

activities.title: An Immigration Officer's Job

content.passage: Every day, people enter the country by road, sea and air. Everybody who is not a citizen of this country must do two things. First, they must fill in a landing card. This tells me a lot about them - where they come from, what their jobs are, why they have come here, and so on. If they didn't fill in this card, we wouldn't know who was in the country. The second thing that they must do is show their passports. In fact, everybody must do this. Passports tell me a lot about people, including the countries they have visited. Every passport must contain a photograph of the owner. Some people must have a visa in their passports. This means that they have special permission to enter the country. If everything is correct, I stamp their passports and wish them a pleasant stay in my country.

activities.title: Direct vs. Indirect Questions

options.feedback: This is the word order for an indirect question or a statement.
Correct! Direct questions often use an auxiliary verb before the subject.

questions.question: In a direct question (like 'Where do you come from?'), what is the typical word order?
questions.explanation: Direct questions usually follow a Verb-Subject word order, often with an auxiliary verb like 'do', 'is', or 'have' coming before the subject.

options.feedback: Correct! Indirect questions use statement word order (Subject-Verb) after the question word.
This is the word order for a direct question.

questions.question: In an indirect question (like 'I'd like to know where you come from.'), what is the typical word order after the question word?
questions.explanation: Indirect questions are embedded within a statement or another question, so they follow the standard Subject-Verb word order.

options.text: Could you tell me what is your job?
options.feedback: This is an indirect question, but the word order at the end is incorrect. It should be '...what your job is'.
Excellent! This is a perfect direct question with Verb ('is') before Subject ('your job').

options.text: I want to know what is your job.
options.feedback: This is an indirect question with incorrect word order at the end.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correctly formed direct question?
questions.explanation: The direct question 'What is your job?' uses the correct Verb-Subject order.

content.transcript:
Officer: Good afternoon. May I see your passport and landing card, please?
Visitor: Yes, of course. Here you are.
Officer: Thank you. I see you've arrived from Dubai. What is the purpose of your visit to the UK?
Visitor: I'm here for a holiday.
Officer: And what is your occupation, sir?
Visitor: I'm an engineer.
Officer: An engineer. Okay. And where will you be staying in the UK?
Visitor: I'll be at the Park Hotel in London. The address is on the card.
Officer: I see it. Everything seems to be in order. Enjoy your stay.
Visitor: Thank you very much.

activities.title: Reading: A Responsible Job

content.passage:
Reporter: You work at the airport, Abla, don't you?
Abla: That's right. I work in security.
Reporter: What exactly do you do?
Abla: Everybody who goes on a plane must be checked. It's my job to search ladies' hand luggage. I must make sure that there is nothing dangerous in their bags.
Reporter: How do you do that?
Abla: All the bags are X-rayed. If we see anything we're not sure of, we open them.
Reporter: So, it's a very responsible job?
Abla: Yes, it is. It means that you have to be very careful all the time. You can't relax.
Reporter: What do you do after work?
Abla: Watch TV. Visit my friends.
Reporter: What do they think about your job?
Abla: They tease me. They tell me I'm too small to be a policewoman.
Reporter: And your family?
Abla: They think it's great. In fact, it was my mother who suggested that I join the police.
Reporter: So you enjoy your job?
Abla: Very much. I enjoy the responsibility. I make people feel safe. That makes me feel good.
Reporter: Any ambitions?
Abla: Yes. I'd like to continue with my education and maybe join the air-wing.
Reporter: So you'll stay in the police?
Abla: Definitely. If I left the police, I wouldn't be happy.

activities.title: Practice the Verb Forms

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: If you look in the top drawer, you ___ your keys. (see)
sentences.explanation: This is a likely situation (Type 1), so we use 'will see'.

sentences.text: If I had his phone number, I ___ him. (meet)
sentences.explanation: The 'if' clause is in the past tense ('had'), so this is an unlikely situation (Type 2). We use 'would meet'.

sentences.text: If I were you, I ___ more careful. (be)
sentences.explanation: This is an impossible situation used for giving advice (Type 2), so we use 'would be'.

sentences.text: If he ___ less, he would be healthier. (eat)
sentences.explanation: The result clause uses 'would be', so the 'if' clause must be in the past tense for a Type 2 conditional. The answer is 'ate'.

sentences.text: If I ___ to London, I would visit the British Museum. (go)
sentences.explanation: The result clause 'I would visit' indicates a Type 2 conditional, so the 'if' clause needs the past tense verb 'went'.

activities.title: It's All Part of the Job

content.passage:
Fuad Rashid is a fireman. Here, he is talking about the work of the fire brigade.

Putting out fires is not the only thing we do in the fire brigade. We give advice on fire prevention and we give advice on what to do if there is a fire. We are often called to traffic accidents to help the traffic police. And then there are the unexpected jobs, all different.

Helping at traffic accidents is another part of our job. Maybe the car is on fire. We put it out. Sometimes people are trapped in the car and we have to cut them free. This often makes me angry because a lot of accidents are unnecessary. They are caused by bad driving.

Giving advice is an important part of our job. We check buildings and point out things that could start a fire. We also make sure that there are enough fire extinguishers. We make recommendations about safety equipment such as fireproof doors and smoke-alarms. In a burning building, smoke can be as dangerous as fire, so we tell people what to do about smoke. We also carry out fire-drill practice.

Last week, we were called to a house. A little boy had been saying goodbye to his father when he put his head through the bars of the gate and couldn't get it out again. We had to bend the bars to free him. It's all part of the job. In the fire brigade, we have to be ready for the unexpected.

activities.title: Fire Destroys School

content.passage:
Article 1:
Fire completely destroyed a school in Salah yesterday. When the fire-engines arrived from nearby Taiz, the fire was blazing out of control. 'We couldn't save the school. But we pointed our hoses at the houses next to the school,' said Fireman Rashid, 'and we saved them.' One fireman was injured and had to be rushed to hospital.

Article 2:
A fireman from Taiz ran into the flames of a blazing school yesterday evening to save the caretaker, who was asleep. The fireman's hands were badly burned and he is now in hospital. Luckily the caretaker was not injured. The fire completely destroyed the primary school in Salah. Two fire-engines rushed to the scene from nearby Taiz, but the fire was already out of control. However, the fire brigade were able to save the houses next to the school. Fireman Fuad Rashid said the fire was probably started by an electrical fault.

content.transcript:
Presenter: A fishing boat is missing. Nobody knows where it is. The boat, with three fishermen in it, left Shuqrah yesterday morning. The boat did not return to Shuqrah yesterday evening. The people in the village were worried. They called the police. Now the police are looking for the missing boat. Here is part of a conversation between a police boat and Police Headquarters.
HQ: Calling Boat 7. Calling Boat 7. Come in, Boat 7. Over!
Boat: Boat 7 here. Boat 7 here. Over!
HQ: Have you seen anything yet? Over!
Boat: No. Nothing. We haven’t seen anything. Over!
HQ: What is your position? Where are you now? Over!
Boat: We’re about 20 kilometres south of Zinjibar. Over!
HQ: What’s the weather like? What’s the weather like? Over!
Boat: It’s bad. Quite bad. And it’s getting worse. There’s a strong wind blowing from the north east. Over!
HQ: Can we do anything? Can we help? Over!
Boat: Yes. Yes, you can. A helicopter would help. Repeat. A helicopter. It’ll be dark in two hours. We must find that fishing boat before then. We’ve got to. Over!
HQ: OK. We’ll call the air-wing. What has happened to the fishing boat? What do you think? What do you think? Over!

content.passage:
Early on Tuesday morning a fishing boat left the village of Shuqrah. The three men on board were Yousif Hassan, his brother, Kamal, and his cousin, Omar. According to Yousif Hassan, the weather was reasonable at the time. They set off towards the fishing grounds, thirty kilometres south of Shuqrah, but they never reached them. About fifteen kilometres out, their engine died. When this had happened on previous occasions, Kamal had always been able to find the fault and repair it. This time, however, the engine was beyond repair. There was nothing they could do except wait to be rescued. As the north-easterly wind grew stronger, they were blown farther and farther out to sea.

Late on Tuesday night when the three men had not returned, their worried families called the police. The next morning a police boat began looking for the missing fishing boat. They searched all day without success. At five o'clock the weather was getting worse and the police asked for help from the air-wing. A police helicopter joined the search and one hour later the pilot, Salman Nasser, found the missing boat. He guided the police boat on his radio and waited until it arrived. The police boat threw a rope to the fishermen and headed back to Shuqrah with the boat in tow. Five hours later, the three men were back with their families. Yousif Hassan told me that although they had begun to get a little worried, they were confident that the police rescue team would find them eventually.

content.passage:
### The United Kingdom
There are four separate countries in the United Kingdom. These are the two kingdoms of England and Scotland, the principality of Wales and the province of Northern Ireland. Each country has its own capital. Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland, Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland and Cardiff is the capital of Wales. London is the capital of England and also of the UK.

### Language
There are three main languages in the UK. English is an official language everywhere, but Welsh is the second official language in Wales. There are radio and TV programmes in Welsh and it is used on road signs and official documents. Gaelic is spoken in parts of Scotland.

### History
The country has been called the United Kingdom only since the beginning of the 19th century. Before that it was called Britain or Great Britain. Wales was united with England in 1282. In 1603 the king of Scotland became the king of all three countries. Ireland became part of the UK in 1801. Southern Ireland became an independent republic in 1921.

### System of government
The United Kingdom is a parliamentary monarchy. This means that the monarch, the king or queen, is the Head of State but has no real power. The king or queen 'reigns', but does not 'rule'. The country is ruled or governed by a parliament. In 1649, after a long Civil War, Britain became a republic. It had no king or queen, but was ruled by a kind of president. It became a monarchy again in 1660.

### The Union Jack
The flag of the United Kingdom, the Union Jack, consists of the flags of England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. It is a symbol of the unity of the country.

### From Empire to Commonwealth
In 1945 the UK was still the head of the British Empire, which covered a quarter of the world's surface. A quarter of the population of the world was governed from London. Most of the countries of the Empire are now independent, but they have stayed members of a kind of international club called the Commonwealth.

activities.title: Reading: Queen Victoria

content.passage:
Queen Victoria's life covers most of the 19th century. She became Queen of the United Kingdom in 1837 when she was only 18 years old. Three years later, she married Albert, a German prince. They had nine children. Albert died in 1861. After his death, Victoria wore black clothes for the rest of her life. She herself died in 1901 at the age of 81 and is the longest reigning British monarch.

People's daily life changed greatly during Victoria's reign. Industry became more important than agriculture and many people moved from the country to towns to work in the new factories. At first the towns were dirty and unhealthy, but slowly things improved. New sewers took away the waste water from people's homes and houses were built with gardens. Big towns had libraries, art galleries and parks. In 1837, only rich people went to school, but by 1901 education was free for everybody up to the age of twelve. Railways were built in every part of the kingdom. People became richer and were able to buy more goods. Hundreds of new shops opened. Covered shopping centres, called arcades, were built in the large towns. Towards the end of the century, large department stores opened. Shoppers could now buy nearly everything they wanted in one step.

The adjective 'Victorian' describes things typical of the time of the Queen's reign. Victorian buildings were often decorated with statues and carved stone. The architecture imitated the style of church buildings of five centuries earlier. Typical Victorian fashion in clothing was floor-length dresses for women and long black coats for men. Victorian values included hard work and strict discipline for children. The saying "children should be seen and not heard" comes from this time.

activities.title: Reading: The Voice of the People

content.passage:
A third large supermarket is to be built on the edge of the town. Johnson's engineering factory is to close next month with the loss of 150 jobs. What do the people of the town think of these changes?

**The New Supermarket**

**Alan Cooper - 45**
I'm completely against the idea of another one. I'm a market-trader. Ten years ago there used to be a good market here in the town centre every day. Now we have a market once a week. Lots of shops have closed as well. It's all because of those supermarkets.

**Jenny Green - 35**
I can't wait for the new supermarket. I'm all for it. It's great to be able to get everything in one shop. It's so convenient. I don't have time to go around to different shops, carrying heavy shopping. I remember shopping in the market. It was very crowded and shopping took ages.

**Johnson's Engineering**

**Sally Woodman - 25**
Johnson's was an old-fashioned factory. It was also a dirty place to work. I'm in favour of it closing. This town needs new industries, like electronics. New factories are cleaner and places to work. I hope the new industries create lots of jobs for women.

**Fred Mason - 55**
I've worked at Johnson's since I was 16. I'm an engineer. I can't do anything else. So, I'm not in favour of it closing. I know that new industries are coming to the town but they're not going to take men from Johnson's. We're all going to have to move to another part of the country to get new jobs.

activities.title: Reading: A Town in Transition

content.passage:
A new out-of-town supermarket is opening, and the old engineering factory is closing, causing mixed reactions among the residents. 

**Alan Cooper**, an elderly resident, is unhappy. 'The new supermarket is too far away, and I don't have a car,' he says. 'Many local shops, like the baker's and the butcher's, have already closed. It's a shame.'

**Jenny Green**, a busy working mother, has a different view. 'I'm looking forward to it! I don't have time to go to different shops. Buying everything I need in one place will be so convenient. They also say we'll soon be able to shop from home using a computer.'

**Sally Woodman** is optimistic about the factory closing. 'It's sad that 150 jobs will be lost, but the factory was old-fashioned. The town needs new industries like electronics. These new industries create jobs for women, which is great for the town's future.'

**Fred Mason**, who worked at the factory, is worried. 'I've worked in engineering my whole life. There are no jobs in these new industries for men like me. I don't know what I'm going to do. Maybe I'll have to dig gardens to earn money.'

activities.title: Reading: The Tower of London

content.passage:
The Tower of London is one of the oldest buildings in the United Kingdom. It stands on the bank of the River Thames in the middle of London. The central tower was built by King William the First in the 11th century to show the power of the King to the people of London. It was painted white in 1241 and since then has been called The White Tower. The outer walls were added in the 12th and 13th centuries.

The building has been used in many different ways. It was first a royal palace where the kings and queens could live safely. Later it was used as a prison for traitors - people who committed serious crimes against the king or country. Prisoners were brought into the tower from the river through a special gate, now called Traitor's Gate. Many prisoners were executed for their crimes. The executioner cut their heads off with an axe.

Nowadays the Tower of London is a museum. Apart from looking at the old building itself, visitors can see many interesting exhibits. The most famous exhibit is the Crown Jewels. This is a set of very valuable jewellery. It is a symbol of the power of the king or queen. The biggest piece is the crown itself, which is put in the head of a new king or queen at a special ceremony called a coronation. The largest diamond in the world, the Star of Africa, is set in another piece of jewellery.

Visitors will also notice that many ravens live in the gardens of the Tower. There is a superstition that the building will collapse and the monarchy will fall if these big black birds ever fly away. The feathers on the ravens' wings are cut to stop this happening.

content.transcript: Guide: (Part 1) Welcome to the Royal Pavilion. We are now in the Entrance Hall. The oldest part of the building you see was once a farmhouse. The Prince, who later became King George the Fourth, bought it in 1785. It was made larger in the years 1801 and 1802. The next big changes happened between 1815 and 1823, when the Pavilion was rebuilt. The inside of the building was decorated in the beautiful Chinese style. The outside, as you can see, was decorated in the Indian style. After King George, his brother, King William, used the Pavilion. He died in 1837. His successor, Queen Victoria, visited Brighton but did not like the Pavilion. She said it was 'a strange, odd, Chinese-looking place, both inside and outside'. She sold it to the town of Brighton in 1850. The rooms you will see on this tour include the breakfast room, dining room, the library, a conservatory, the kitchen, and the music room. (Part 2) ... that was the main dining room with its rich decorations. Now, we are in the Great Kitchen. Stand here, please, ladies and gentlemen. You'll be able to see better. To your left by the wall are the cookers where food was boiled or fried and in front of them some tables where the food was prepared - the preparation tables. This is where meat and vegetables were chopped and sauces made and so on. When the food was cooked, it was put on the big table in front of you - the steam table. The table top is made of metal. Steam from boiling water came along pipes to the space under the top and this is how they kept the food hot before it went into the dining room. To your right is a big fire where the meat was cooked. And on the shelves on the wall in front of you are all the pans. Now if you look up, you will see that the room is very high and that there are a lot of windows. This was to stop the kitchen from getting too hot. We will now go upstairs to Queen Victoria's bedroom. If you would come this way, please. This way, sir. Madam.

activities.title: Reading for Detail: An English Tradition

content.passage:
## An English tradition

**Presenter:** The police want to cancel this year's cheese rolling race. With me to talk about it are John Shepherd and Sergeant Lewis, a local policeman. John Shepherd wants the race to go ahead. Sergeant Lewis doesn't. Mr Shepherd, what is the cheese rolling race?

**John Shepherd:** We roll wheel-shaped cheeses down a hill and about 30 people run down after them and try to catch them.

**Presenter:** Do they ever catch the cheeses?

**John Shepherd:** Never. The winner is the first person to reach the bottom of the hill.

**Presenter:** And you want to stop this race, Sergeant Lewis. Why?

**Sergeant Lewis:** It's just too dangerous. Last year 35 people were injured, some of them people who had just come to watch. The people running down the hill fell and broke their legs or arms. Many were taken to hospital by helicopters and ambulances.

**Presenter:** How were the spectators injured?

**Sergeant Lewis:** These cheeses are heavy - about three kilos - and they go downhill very fast. Sometimes they bounce off the ground into the crowd and cause serious injuries. The race causes too much work for the emergency services. They have better things to do.

**John Shepherd:** I agree that it's dangerous, but nobody has ever been killed and it's very popular. Thousands of people come to watch the races. They've taken place for hundreds of years - some people say since the Romans were here 1,600 years ago - and we don't want to stop it now. It's a tradition.

**Presenter:** But if people are injured, it should be stopped, shouldn't it?

**John Shepherd:** They choose to take part. It's just a bit of fun. We live in a time when people aren't allowed to have fun or to do anything dangerous.

**Sergeant Lewis:** We don't want to stop people having fun. We just want to protect the spectators and prevent injuries. It must be organized better.

**John Shepherd:** We'll see what we can do for next year.

**Presenter:** Mr Shepherd, Sergeant Lewis, thank you.

activities.title: Discovering Scotland

content.passage:
### SCOTLAND
Scotland is the most northern country in the United Kingdom. Although part of the UK, Scotland still has its own legal and educational systems. It also competes independently in international sports, such as football and rugby. In fact, many Scots think that Scotland should become independent again.

### PHYSICAL
There are three main geographical areas in Scotland. The mountainous area in the north is called The Highlands. This area contains the highest mountain in the UK, Ben Nevis, which rises to 1,343 metres above sea level. There are several lochs (lakes) in this area, the best-known one being Loch Ness. A flat plain called The Lowlands crosses the centre of the country. Most of Scotland’s population of about 5,200,000 live here. The third part of Scotland, The Southern Uplands, is hilly. Scotland has many rivers. The Spey and Tay are famous for salmon fishing and the Clyde, which flows through Glasgow, used to be famous for ship-building.

### INCOME
In The Highlands, farming and fishing are the traditional sources of income. Scottish beef is world-famous and Scottish fish is exported to many countries. In the past twenty or thirty years, however, tourism has brought a lot of money into the area. Another important change was caused by the discovery of oil in the North Sea of Scotland. This has created many jobs and changed the lives of many Highlanders. The traditional industries of The Lowlands were coal-mining, ship-building and steel making. These industries have now almost disappeared. New industries include electronics, chemicals and light engineering.

### FAMOUS SCOTS
Scotland has produced many famous people, chiefly engineers and inventors. James Watt, the inventor of the steam engine, was Scottish. The unit of electrical power was named after him. Thomas Telford, another engineer, built the first iron bridge in the world in 1779. In 1926 another Scot, James Logie Baird, invented television. The Scottish doctor, Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. For a small country, Scotland has had a big influence on the world.

prompts.prompt: In the reign of Queen Arwa, many new mosques were built. She died in 1138 at the age of 92.
prompts.explanation: Use 'who' for people. The clause 'who died in 1138 at the age of 92' gives extra information about Queen Arwa.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Have been' in the answer matches the present perfect 'have you been' in the question.

questions.explanation: The answer 'I've been on holiday' uses the present perfect tense. The question 'Where have you been?' also uses the present perfect to ask about a recent past experience.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple 'went' in the answer matches the past simple 'did you go' in the question.
Incorrect. 'Have you been' is present perfect, but the answer 'I went' is past simple, referring to a completed trip.

options.feedback: This is a possible question, but 'What were the people like?' is a more common way to ask for a description.

activities.title: Life on a Ranch

content.passage:
Hi Sam,

Life here is very different from the city. We live on a huge sheep ranch in a rural area, miles from any town. The original settlers in this region arrived over 150 years ago. They learned a lot from the local Aborigines about how to survive in this tough environment. Our farm is so big that we use a small plane to check on the sheep. It's a lot of hard work, but it's a peaceful life. The population density is incredibly low; you can go for days without seeing another person! It’s a beautiful place, isn't it? I wouldn't want to live anywhere else.

Best,
Charlie

activities.title: Reading: An Introduction to Australia

content.passage:
Australia is bounded by the Indian Ocean on the west and south and by the Pacific Ocean on the east. It is the smallest of the continents, but it is the sixth largest country in the world. However, the population is only 17 million, so its population density is very low. There are only 2.1 people for every square kilometre (km²). About 85% of the population live in urban areas - towns and cities. Canberra is the capital of Australia, but Sydney is the biggest city. It also has the most famous building in Australia - the Sydney Opera House.

The Aborigines were the first people to live in Australia, long before the Europeans discovered it. They are dark-skinned people, probably originally from south-east Asia. They arrived in Australia about 40,000 years ago. They were nomads, moving from place to place. The only weapons they had were wooden spears and boomerangs. They depended on hunting, fishing and gathering wild plants for their food. There were many different tribes, each living in a different part of the country and each with its own tribal language. The tribes lived peacefully with each other and respected the land they lived on.

However, things changed about 200 years ago when the first European settlers arrived in Australia. Most of the settlers were from Britain or Ireland. They set up farms to raise sheep and cattle. Quite often, these farms were on land used by the Aborigines. This led to fights between the Aborigines and the settlers. The Aborigines had no chance with their wooden spears against the settlers' guns. Large numbers were killed. Many more died from diseases brought into the country by the settlers because they had no natural protection against these diseases. Today, the Aborigines make up only 1% of the population of Australia. Their nomadic way of life has gone; they are no longer free to move from place to place. However, they still use their tribal languages as well as English, which is the official language of the country.

When most people think of Australia, they think of sheep. This is because Australia has about 15% of the world's population of sheep. In fact, for every person in Australia there are ten sheep. Some of the sheep ranches are huge and they can be hundreds of kilometres from the nearest town or city. They can also be a long way from the nearest tarmac road, so the farmers travel on dirt roads. These roads turn into mud when it rains. For this reason, most ranches have a landing strip for small planes. If a farmer becomes seriously ill, he depends on the famous Flying Doctor Service to help him.

activities.title: Discovering Australia

content.passage:
Australia, the sixth largest country in the world, is a continent of contrasts. Surrounded by the Indian and Pacific oceans, it is a vast land, yet it has one of the lowest population densities in the world, with only about 2.2 people per square kilometer. While the country is huge, about 85% of the population lives in urban areas, mostly along the coast. The capital city is Canberra, but the largest cities are Sydney and Melbourne.

The original inhabitants are the Aborigines, who came from Southeast Asia thousands of years ago. They lived a nomadic, tribal lifestyle until the arrival of European settlers, mostly from Britain and Ireland. This arrival was a disaster for the Aborigines, who suffered greatly from new diseases and superior weapons like guns. Today, they make up only about 1% of the population.

Life outside the cities, in the 'outback', can be tough. Huge farms, called ranches or stations, raise sheep and cattle. For every person in Australia, there are about ten sheep! Roads are often unpaved dirt tracks, and if a farmer becomes seriously ill, they depend on the famous Flying Doctor Service.

activities.title: India and the Taj Mahal

content.passage:
India is bounded by three seas. The Bay of Bengal is to the east, the India Ocean to the south and the Arabian Sea to the west. About 200 different languages are spoken in India. Hindi and English are the official languages. The population, which was 683 million in 1981, increases by about 13 million every year. Eighty-three per cent of Indians are Hindus, 11% are Muslims and 3% are Christians.

India is the world's largest producer of tea. Tea comes from the leaves of the tea plant. Most of the tea is grown in the north of India because the climate is cooler than in the rest of the country. The most famous tea comes from an area around the town of Darjeeling. Darjeeling tea is known around the world.

## The Taj Mahal

The Taj Mahal is one of the most beautiful buildings in the world. It is the story of Shah Jahan and his wife, Mumtaz Mahal. Shah Jahan was an Emperor of India in the 17th century. In 1628, he made himself Emperor. His happiness ended in 1631 when Mumtaz died giving birth to their fourteenth child.

Shah Jahan was filled with grief. He took his wife's body to the city of Agra and buried it in a beautiful garden. Then he began to build her tomb, the Taj Mahal beside the river Jumna. The stone he used was white marble. It took him 20 years to build the tomb. When it was finished, he buried the body of his wife in the Taj Mahal. Then he decided to build a copy of the Taj Mahal for himself. It would be made of black marble on the other side of the river. However, this never happened.

content.passage: Shah Jahan was a Mughal emperor in India. He had two older brothers. To get the support of the people, he travelled around India. In 1612, he married Mumtaz Mahal. In 1628, his father died and he became emperor. Mumtaz Mahal was Queen of India for three years. She died in 1631 while giving birth. Shah Jahan's grief was so great that he decided to build the most beautiful tomb in the world for her. The Taj Mahal is made of white marble and is located next to the Jumna river. It took 20 years to build and was finished in 1651. Mumtaz Mahal was first buried in a garden before being moved to the completed tomb.
