content.transcript: Jim: Mark! I haven't seen you for weeks. Where have you been? Mark: I've been on holiday. Jim: Where did you go? Mark: To East Africa. Jim: That's Kenya, isn't it? Mark: No, it's Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. Jim: And you went to all three, did you? Mark: No, only two. I didn't go to Uganda. Jim: Where did you go first? Mark: Well, I flew to Nairobi. That's the capital of Kenya. I spent three days there. Then I drove to Mombasa. I stayed in a hotel near the beach right on the Indian Ocean. Jim: That sounds great! Mark: It was. I spent ten days swimming, fishing and just lying in the sun. Jim: What were the local people like? Mark: Very nice. Very friendly. Most of them speak English. Jim: Really? Mark: Yes. Swahili and English are both official languages. Of course, there are many tribal languages as well. Jim: So, ten days in Mombasa. What did you do next? Mark: I spent five days in the Serengeti National Park. That's over the border, in Tanzania. Jim: I've heard about Serengeti. It's full of wild animals, isn't it? Mark: Oh, yes. Elephants, lions, leopards, buffaloes, all sorts of deer... Jim: And you saw all of them, did you? Mark: No, not all. Most of them. I didn't see any leopards. Jim: Oh, that's pity. Mark: The best part of the holiday was the two days I spent with the Masai tribe. Jim: Oh, I've read about them. They're nomads, aren't they? Mark: Yes. They have lots of cows, so they go where their cows can feed. Jim: And they have those long spears, don't they? Mark: That's right. They use them to protect their cows from wild animals - lions mostly. Jim: These spears - what are they like? Mark: Well, they're about two metres long. They're in three parts. The middle part is the handle. It's made of wood. On one end of the handle, there's a long straight blade with two sharp edges. On the other end, there's a long spike. Jim: You didn't bring one back, did you? Mark: No! How could I get one on a plane? Anyway, the Masai wouldn't sell you one. They need them. Jim: It sounds like you had a great time. Mark: You could say that.

activities.title: Reading for Detail: Mark's Trip

content.passage:
Jim: Mark! I haven't seen you for weeks. Where have you been?

Mark: I've been on holiday.

Jim: Where did you go?

Mark: To East Africa.

Jim: That's Kenya, isn't it?

Mark: No, it's Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Jim: And you went to all three, did you?

Mark: No, only two. I didn't go to Uganda.

Jim: Where did you go first?

Mark: Well, I flew to Nairobi. That's the capital of Kenya. I spent three days there. Then I drove to Mombasa. I stayed in a hotel near the beach right on the Indian Ocean.

Jim: That sounds great!

Mark: It was. I spent ten days swimming, fishing and just lying in the sun.

Jim: What were the local people like?

Mark: Very nice. Very friendly. Most of them speak English.

Jim: Really?

Mark: Yes. Swahili and English are both official languages. Of course, there are many tribal languages as well.

Jim: So, ten days in Mombasa. What did you do next?

Mark: I spent five days in the Serengeti National Park. That's over the border, in Tanzania.

Jim: I've heard about Serengeti. It's full of wild animals, isn't it?

Mark: Oh, yes. Elephants, lions, leopards, buffaloes, all sorts of deer...

Jim: And you saw all of them, did you?

Mark: No, not all. Most of them. I didn't see any leopards.

Jim: Oh, that's pity.

Mark: The best part of the holiday was the two days I spent with the Masai tribe.

Jim: Oh, I've read about them. They're nomads, aren't they?

Mark: Yes. They have lots of cows, so they go where their cows can feed.

Jim: And they have those long spears, don't they?

Mark: That's right. They use them to protect their cows from wild animals - lions mostly.

Jim: These spears - what are they like?

Mark: Well, they're about two metres long. They're in three parts. The middle part is the handle. It's made of wood. On one end of the handle, there's a long straight blade with two sharp edges. On the other end, there's a long spike.

Jim: You didn't bring one back, did you?

Mark: No! How could I get one on a plane? Anyway, the Masai wouldn't sell you one. They need them.

Jim: It sounds like you had a great time.

Mark: You could say that.

content.passage:
Canada is the second largest country in the world. It has an area of more than 9 million square kilometres. However, it has a population of only 30 million, one tenth the population of the United States of America, which is smaller than Canada. Its population density is 3.3 people per km², one of the lowest in the world. Only about 10% of Canada is settled. Most Canadians live in the south, within 100 kilometres of the border with the USA. Very few people live in the north of Canada because it is covered by snow and ice for most of the year.

Canada has two official languages, English and French. Sixty-seven percent of the people speak only English, 18% speak only French, 13.5% speak both languages and 1.5% speak neither language. Most Canadians are Christian.

activities.title: A Canadian Legend: Raven and the Light

content.passage: Raven sat in a tree. It was dark and had been dark for as long as he could remember. He could not see anything. He could not even see himself because all his feathers were black. Raven was not happy. Then he heard a rumour about an old fisherman who lived by the sea with his young daughter. The girl's mother had died a few years earlier. According to the rumour, the fisherman had a ball of light hidden in his house. The Raven decided to steal the light and set it free in the world. He flew to a fruit tree near the fisherman's house. He knew that the fisherman's daughter came to collect the fruit. Raven flew down to the ground. Then he changed himself into a baby boy and waited. When the girl arrived at the tree, she was amazed to see the baby. She picked it up and ran back to the house. As soon as the old man saw the baby, he fell in love with him. 'We don't know where this child came from, but we must take care of him,' he said to his daughter. 'From now on, he is my grandson.' The baby grew and grew. The old man loved him and gave him everything he wanted. One day, the boy began to cry for the ball of light that was kept in a box. At first the old man would not give it to him, but he cried and cried. In the end, the old man said to his daughter, 'Give my grandson what he is asking for. Give him the ball of light.' His daughter got the box and took out the ball of light. 'Here's your light,' she said, throwing it to the child. Immediately, Raven changed himself back into his real shape and flew out of the house with the ball of light in his beak. As he was flying away, he was chased by a huge eagle. The eagle made him drop the ball of light. It fell and broke into many pieces. The large pieces became the Sun and the Moon and the smaller ones became the stars in the night sky.

content.passage:
In the distant past, the world was dark. The native people, the Inuit, lived in darkness. Raven, a famous character in their legends, was unhappy with the dark. He heard a rumour that an old fisherman who lived by the sea had a ball of light, which was hidden in a box.

Raven wanted to set the light free. He changed himself into a baby and waited near the fisherman's house. The fisherman's daughter found the baby and took him home to take care of him. The baby was Raven, and he grew and grew. He cried all the time, and the only thing that made him stop was looking at the box with the light. In the end, the old man, his grandfather, gave him the ball of light to play with.

As soon as Raven had the ball, he changed back into a bird and flew out of the house with the light in his beak. He flew high into the sky. He was so high that he looked like an eagle. He dropped the ball, and it broke into pieces. The biggest piece became the moon, and the smaller pieces became the stars, filling the sky with light.

activities.title: Reading: New York City

content.passage:
New York is the largest city in the United States of America. It is made up of a number of parts, most of which are on islands. The main part of New York, the centre, is on an island called Manhattan.

The original inhabitants of Manhattan were American Indians who had arrived there thousands of years before the first European settlers. In 1626, a Dutchman called Peter Minuit bought the island from the Indians for 24 dollars. In those days, Manhattan was rural. Today, Manhattan is completely urban except for a large park called Central Park and a few smaller parks. The population density of Manhattan is very high. About 25,000 people per km². Because so many people wanted to live in such a small place, they had to build upwards instead of outwards. That is why Manhattan has so many very tall buildings. They are called skyscrapers.

One of the most famous sights in New York is the Statue of Liberty. It is, perhaps, the most famous statue in the world. It is certainly one of the biggest. It is over 46 metres high and its right arm is nearly 13 metres long. You can go up inside the statue. First you take a lift and then you must walk 168 steps to the crown. From the top, there are magnificent views of New York City.

The Statue of Liberty was given to the United States by the people of France in 1866. It was placed on a stone and concrete base on an island in New York harbour. During the last hundred years, millions of people left their own countries to start a new life in America. They came from Europe, Asia, South America and Africa. For most of these immigrants, the Statue of Liberty was the first thing they saw in their new home. Today, the great-grandchildren of these immigrants make New York one of the most multi-racial cities in the world.

activities.title: Reading: Barry's Christmas Dinner

content.passage:
Chemistry used to be my favourite subject. That was before the lesson last Wednesday. Kevin put his hand up. 'Yes, Smith?' said Mr Law. 'Sir, Jones is on fire,' said Kevin. 'Well, put him out!' 'Wham!' I shouted as Kevin threw water all over me. 'Your pullover was on fire,' he explained. 'You were standing too close to the flame of that Bunsen burner.'
Mum was not very pleased when I got home. 'That was such a lovely Christmas present from your Aunt Joan,' she said. 'Now look at it! You've only had it for a couple of months.'
I will never forget last Christmas. On Christmas Eve we all went to church and sang some carols. At about two o'clock on Christmas Day everything was ready for dinner. The turkey and all the vegetables were cooked. They looked and smelled fantastic. Mum asked me to take all the food into the dining room. 'That's easy,' I thought.
Ten minutes later everything looked different. First I burned my hand on a hot pan. I screamed. Sue put a bandage on. Then I spilled some sauce on the other hand and screamed again. Sue put another bandage on.
As I was coming into the dining room with the turkey, I slipped on something and fell backwards. The turkey flew for the first time in its life. The plate broke on the floor. Fortunately, I did catch the bird. Unfortunately, it banged my head on the floor. Sue got another bandage on. Dad was very angry because his best sweater was covered with turkey fat. Mum said 'Merry Christmas' to herself several times. Sue laughed all through the dinner and I had a headache.
'What do you want for your birthday, Barry?' asked Kevin the next day. 'A new pullover,' I said.

activities.title: Reading: An Interview on Tourism

content.passage:
Tourism is important to the development of any country. It brings foreign currencies into the country. In fact, in some countries, it is the only way of earning hard currencies such as the US dollar or the German mark. Our reporter interviewed an official from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism to get his views on tourism in our country.

**Reporter:** What is the situation on tourism at the moment?
**Official:** The situation is promising. Sixty thousand tourists visited the country in 1995. That number increased to 75,000 in 1996. In that year, we earned 45 million dollars from tourism.

**Reporter:** That's good, isn't it?
**Official:** Yes, but it's not good enough. We need even hundreds of millions of dollars because we have so much to offer. There are countries that offer much less, but they get many more tourists than we do.

**Reporter:** What's the reason for this?
**Official:** Quite simply, people don't know about us. For example, most Americans don't know where Yemen is and they don't know anything about the attractions of this country. If they did, they would come here in their thousands bringing their dollars with them.

**Reporter:** So, what's the answer?
**Official:** There is more than one answer. We have to promote the tourist industry. We have to advertise. We have a very rich historical and cultural heritage. Our archaeological sites tell the history of Yemen's past. Our handicrafts are unique - there's nothing like them anywhere else in the world. We also have wonderful scenery. Our coastline is more than 2,000 kilometres long with many beautiful beaches. Our mountains are magnificent and they are full of wild life of all kinds. When the rest of the world learns about all these things, we'll have a powerful tourist industry.

**Reporter:** You said there was more than one answer.
**Official:** Yes. When people come here, they have to have somewhere to stay. So we have to build more four - and five - star hotels. We have to develop our airports. We have to improve some of our roads so that tourists can get up into the mountains, to the archeological sites and to the most beautiful parts of our rural areas.

**Reporter:** But all this would cost a lot of money, wouldn't it?
**Official:** Yes, but it would be money well spent. Remember that tourism is an industry. You have to invest money in any industry if you want to make a profit.

**Reporter:** Is there anything else we should do?
**Official:** Yes. We should use the television, radio and newspapers to let our own people know about the benefits of tourism. Tourism means more jobs for everybody. It also means that we have to protect our environment. If our environment is damaged or destroyed, tourism will collapse. We can't let that happen.

statements.statement: We use 'had to' for obligations in the past.
statements.explanation: Correct. We cannot use 'must' for past obligations, so we use 'had to'.

statements.statement: 'You don't have to come' means 'You are not allowed to come'.
statements.explanation: Incorrect. 'Don't have to' means there is no obligation or necessity. 'Must not' means something is not allowed.

statements.statement: 'Must' and 'have to' can both be used for present and future obligations.
statements.explanation: Correct. For example: 'You must work harder' or 'You will have to work harder'.

statements.statement: 'You mustn't talk' means it is not necessary to talk.
statements.explanation: Incorrect. 'Mustn't talk' means talking is not allowed (prohibition). 'Don't have to talk' means it is not necessary.

content.transcript: Salma: Well, what do you think? Laila: It was a very good programme. Salma: No, that's not what I meant. What do you think about all these tourists coming to Yemen? Faysal: I think it's a great idea. I like it. Saleh: I'm not sure. In fact, I don't think it's a good idea. Salma: Why not? Faysal: Hey! What about me? I spoke first. Laila: Yes, but you're the youngest, so you should speak last. Faysal: That's not fair. Anyway, you're only a year older than me. Laila: What's that got to do with it? Salma: Stop it, you two! Why don't you think it's a good idea, Saleh? Saleh: Well, we have our own religion, our own customs and habits. What happens when we get all these tourists coming in with their different religions, different habits and so on? I just worry a bit. Salma: You don't need to worry, Saleh. Our religion and our culture are strong. Tourists aren't going to damage those. Faysal: That's right. You tell him, Salma! Laila: I'm in favour of tourism. We need the hard currency it will bring in. Faysal: What's hard currency? Laila: See! You don't know anything. Salma: Stop it, Laila! A hard currency is one that's used in international trading, like the American dollar, the German mark, the Swiss franc, the British pound, the... Saleh: What's wrong with our riyals? Salma: Nothing. But if we want to buy something from abroad, we have to pay in a hard currency. We can't pay in riyals. Laila: That's right. So, if tourists come here, they'll change their dollars, say, into riyals. And they'll spend their riyals here. So we'll get the riyals back, and we'll also have the dollars to pay for our imports. Faysal: That sounds good to me. But I want tourists to come here so that I can meet them. Saleh: How are you going to meet them? They'll be in their hotels, or on tourist buses. Faysal: But they'll go to the souk to buy things. I'll meet them there. Saleh: How? Faysal: Easy! I'll go up to them and introduce myself in English. Saleh: What if they're French or German? Faysal: No problem. French and German children learn English in school, like me. I'll ask them what it's like to live in their countries. I want to know. Laila: Salma, you haven't said anything about tourism. What do you think? Salma: I'm for it, but for a different reason. Laila: What's your reason? Salma: I'm proud of my country. It's an old and a beautiful country. And we, for example, may be richer than us in some ways, but we are richer than them in history and culture. I'd like them to come here and learn about us. It's as simple as that.

activities.title: Reading: What's Your Opinion?

content.passage:
There are four children in the Al-Oudi family: Salma (19), Saleh (17), Laila (15) and Faysal (14). They have been watching a programme about the development of tourism in Yemen. Now they are talking about it.

**Salma:** Well, what do you think?
**Laila:** It was a very good programme.
**Salma:** No, that's not what I meant. What do you think about all these tourists coming to Yemen?
**Faysal:** I think it's a great idea. I like it.
**Saleh:** I'm not sure. In fact, I don't think it's a good idea.
**Salma:** Why not?
**Faysal:** Hey! What about me? I spoke first.
**Laila:** Yes, but you're the youngest, so you should speak last.
**Faysal:** That's not fair. Anyway, you're only a year older than me.
**Laila:** What's that got to do with it?
**Salma:** Stop it, you two! Why don't you think it's a good idea, Saleh?
**Saleh:** Well, we have our own religion, our own customs and habits. What happens when we get all these tourists coming in with their different religions, different habits and so on? I just worry a bit.
**Salma:** You don't need to worry, Saleh. Our religion and our culture are strong. Tourists aren't going to damage those.
**Faysal:** That's right. You tell him, Salma!
**Laila:** I'm in favour of tourism. We need the hard currency it will bring in.
**Faysal:** What's hard currency?
**Laila:** See! You don't know anything.
**Salma:** Stop it, Laila! A hard currency is one that's used in international trading, like the American dollar, the German mark, the Swiss franc, the British pound, the...
**Saleh:** What's wrong with our riyals?
**Salma:** Nothing. But if we want to buy something from abroad, we have to pay in a hard currency. We can't pay in riyals.
**Laila:** That's right. So, if tourists come here, they'll change their dollars, say, into riyals. And they'll spend their riyals here. So we'll get the riyals back, and we'll also have the dollars to pay for our imports.
**Faysal:** That sounds good to me. But I want tourists to come here so that I can meet them.
**Saleh:** How are you going to meet them? They'll be in their hotels, or on tourist buses.
**Faysal:** But they'll go to the souk to buy things. I'll meet them there.
**Saleh:** How?
**Faysal:** Easy! I'll go up to them and introduce myself in English.
**Saleh:** What if they're French or German?
**Faysal:** No problem. French and German children learn English in school, like me. I'll ask them what it's like to live in their countries. I want to know.
**Laila:** Salma, you haven't said anything about tourism. What do you think?
**Salma:** I'm for it, but for a different reason.
**Laila:** What's your reason?
**Salma:** I'm proud of my country. It's an old and a beautiful country. And we, for example, may be richer than us in some ways, but we are richer than them in history and culture. I'd like them to come here and learn about us. It's as simple as that.

content.passage:
Karl: Right! Is everything arranged?
Helga: Yes. We'll arrive in Sana'a on March the sixth. We stay the night at the Sheraton Hotel and we fly to Riyan the next day.
Karl: Riyan? That's the airport for Mukalla, isn't it?
Helga: Yes, it is. We'll spend three days in Mukalla. On one of those we'll go to Shibam.
Karl: Shibam! Ah, yes. That's the town with the wonderful old houses. I'm looking forward to seeing those.
Helga: After three days we take a taxi to Aden. It's a long drive, but the coastline is wonderful.
Karl: I'm going to buy a djambia in Aden.
Helga: Why Aden? You can buy a djambia in any big town.
Karl: A friend told me the best place to go in Aden.
Helga: All right. After Aden we drive to Taiz and we spend two days there.
Karl: And we must visit Mokha.
Helga: There isn't much left there, is there?
Karl: Maybe not. But I want to see it. After all, it's where coffee came from originally and you know how I like my cup of coffee.
Helga: We're also going to Jibla to see the Great Mosque and Queen Arwa's tomb. She's buried in the grounds of the mosque, you know!
Helga: Then it's back to Sana'a, where we have three days. And that's the end of the holiday.
Karl: But we don't get to see anywhere north of Sana'a.
Helga: We can't go everywhere in less than two weeks. But we can always come back next year.
Karl: Good idea!

activities.title: Reading: My Dream

content.passage:
I was born in a small village south of Hodeida eighteen years ago. There are only two children in my family, my older brother and myself. My brother is 22 years old and is already the captain of his own fishing boat. He bought his boat a year ago. To do this, he used his money and he borrowed some more from the bank. He works on the boat with a crew of three. His three crewmen are all young men like himself and all come from the same village. My brother has a lot of responsibility. He has to pay his crewmen and he has to pay back the money he owes to the bank. When he has done that, he does not have much money left. I will do things differently.

My dream is to have my own boat. I can already see it in my mind. It will be an open boat, five and a half metres long and one and a half metres wide. It will have an outboard motor. However, unlike my brother, I won't have a crew on the boat. I won't use it for fishing, or, at least, I won't be doing the fishing. I will use it to take tourists fishing. Why? Fishing is a hard life. If you don't catch fish to sell, you won't make any money. On the other hand, if you take tourists fishing, you will get your money before you leave the shore. They hire your boat and you take them out to sea. If the tourists catch a lot of fish, they will be very happy. If they don't catch many fish, they will still be happy because they will have had a good day out on the sea.

And it is not just fishing. Tourists like to swim and lie in the sun. There are many islands off the coast of Yemen and I can take tourists to one of them in the morning. I can even supply them with packed lunches. When they are ready to come home, I can go back and pick them up. They will pay me for the use of my boat. I can't lose and it is easier than fishing.

If all goes well, I will buy a bigger boat and then another and another. By the time I am 25 years old, I hope to have a good business. I am not sure where this business will be. There are wonderful beaches in the Hadhramaut between Mukalla and Aden. I might work from there. Who knows? Will all this happen or is it just a dream? Again, who knows?

activities.title: Reading: Nadia's Dream

content.passage:
Nadia is just fifteen. However, like Umar, she knows exactly what she wants to do when she leaves school.

**My Dream**

You probably won't believe this. My friends at school certainly don't believe it. They think I am mad because I want to keep bees. I want to be a beekeeper. That is my dream.

It all began when I was eleven years old. I went to visit my uncle who lives in Egypt. He is a beekeeper and I went with him when he visited his beehives. What I saw was amazing! It was then that I decided to be a beekeeper and I haven't changed my mind. If I tell you what I learned about bees, maybe you will understand why I am fascinated by them.

There are three kinds of bees in a beehive. There are more than 10,000 worker bees. They are sexless - they are neither male nor female. They make the honey and protect the hive. There is a small number of drones. They are male and one of them will mate with the Queen. When that happens, all the drones are thrown out of the hive and they die. There is only one Queen. She is female and she lays thousands and thousands of eggs. The amazing thing is that queen bees are made. The grub, the early stage of a worker bee, will be a worker bee if nothing is done to it. However, if the other worker bees feed it with a substance called Royal Jelly, it will turn into a queen bee.

I will start with two beehives. However, I will have to be careful. I will have to watch out for ants. Ants love sweet things and they can clean out a beehive in one day. However, ants don't swim. Therefore I will put my beehives on small tables. Each table will have four legs. I will put the legs of the tables in tin cans and fill each can with a mixture of water and oil. That should stop the ants.

I hope to get about 20 kilograms of honey from each hive one yield and I hope to get three yields during one year. I will sell my honey to the big hotels. I know they use honey from other countries now, but I think they will be happy to use my Yemeni honey instead. If all goes well, I will get more and more beehives. When that happens, I will sell my honey directly to tourists.

That is my dream and it gives me a buzz. Do you get it?

activities.title: Towards a Greener Land

content.passage:
The Forestry Directorate is part of the Ministry of Agriculture. It has a very important part to play in Yemen's future because it is responsible for forestation and for fighting desertification. Forestation stops the disappearance of trees and plants and makes sure that there are more trees for the future. Desertification is the process by which fertile land is turned into desert. At the moment, about 95% of the country is desert. The remaining 5% is also in danger of turning into desert.

Trees are very important because they have direct effects on the environment. On the side of a mountain, for example, trees prevent the topsoil being washed away by heavy rains. This is called soil erosion. Trees also slow down the flood waters, giving the water time to soak into the soil. Because of soil erosion, farmers cannot grow plants. As a result, more erosion takes place because, like trees, plants also hold the soil together.

Trees also have indirect effects on the environment. Bacteria live in the roots of trees. These bacteria increase the amount of nitrogen in the soil and make the soil more fertile. In areas surrounded by deserts, trees act as wind-breaks. They prevent the wind from moving sand dunes onto fertile soil. Trees also release oxygen into the atmosphere, cool down the environment and provide shade for people and animals.

Desertification happens when trees and plants disappear. Trees and plants need water, which we can get by drilling wells. However, if we drill wells too close together, the water will disappear. This is because a number of wells use up the underground water quicker than one well does. When a well runs dry, the farmer moves on and the area he leaves behind becomes desert. Another cause of desertification is the growth of towns and cities. As they grow, people move onto what used to be agricultural land. This causes more erosion.

Many people either do not know that there is a problem, or do not know the causes. We must educate them. If they understand the problem, they will do something to solve it. In fact, some people are already trying to do this. In the Hadhramaut, for example, people put fertiliser on a piece of land. Then it is protected for six months. No grazing by animals, no cutting of trees or bushes is allowed on protected land until it is ready to be used again. Another tribal custom allows people to cut off only the dead branches and save the rest of the tree.

content.passage:
Desertification is a serious problem, and several factors are responsible for it. One major cause is the disappearance of trees and other plants, which hold the soil together. Another is that farmers are often forced to leave their land because there is no water for their crops. Finally, as towns and cities become bigger, they expand into areas that were once green. 

Fortunately, people are trying to solve this problem. In some areas, land is protected for six months at a time. During this period, animals are not allowed on the land for grazing, and trees or bushes must not be cut. This allows the natural vegetation to recover. Another rule is that people can only cut dead branches from trees for firewood. This protects the living trees, which are vital for the environment. Trees help prevent flood waters from running off the land too quickly, allowing more water to soak into the ground and make the soil fertile. They also act as a wind-break and put oxygen into the air.

activities.title: Exploring Business Ideas

content.passage:
More and more tourists are coming to our country every year. That means more and more jobs and more business opportunities. Who for? Why not you? Just think about it. Then go for it.

We're building new hotels. New hotels mean plenty of new jobs. Aim for the best jobs. Take a course in hotel management, or go on a cookery course and learn how to be a chef. There are other good jobs in a hotel. Find out what they are.

Tourists from colder countries travel to countries that have lots of sunshine. They like to lie on the beach and relax. They want to be comfortable on the beach. If it gets too hot, they want to lie in the shade. Sometimes they get hot and thirsty, or just a little bit hungry. What could you hire out to them? What could you sell to them?

Hang-gliding is a worldwide sport. People strap themselves to a hang-glider, jump off a high mountain and soar like a bird. Kenya is ideal for hang-gliding. We've got the mountains, so why not set up a business? First, you need to learn how to hang-glide yourself. Next, you have to go on a course so that you can teach other people how to hang-glide. Then you're ready.

An easy one-person business is being a tourist guide. You don't have to invest any money. You have to be able to speak English. You have to know everything about your area - its history, its culture, its wildlife, its most beautiful areas, even the best places to take photographs. You have to be able to talk non-stop. Tourists will pay for these skills.

Hundreds of thousands of people around the world are fascinated by birds. They are known as bird-watchers. They will go anywhere to see birds they haven't seen before in the wild. Now there's an opportunity! Learn about all the birds in your area. Find out where they live and nest. Then go for it!

content.transcript: It was May 22nd - my birthday! 'Happy birthday, dear,' said Mum when I got downstairs. 'The postman's just been. There are some cards for you. And there's a nice surprise.' 'What is it?' I asked. 'You'll find out tonight,' said Mum. 'At your party.' On the bus to school, I tried to read my Chemistry book because Mr Law was giving us a test. But I couldn't think about Chemistry. I was thinking about my surprise. What could it be? 'What do you think it is?' I asked Kevin when I got to school. 'The Crown Jewels?' he suggested. The bell went. The Chemistry test began. The Chemistry test finished. I had answered one question. I was still thinking about my surprise. 'I came top today,' said Sue when I got home. 'We had a test in Chemistry and I came top.' I didn't say anything about my test. 'And I've made you a cake.' At the party later, Sue brought the cake in with sixteen candles on it and everybody sang, 'Happy birthday, dear Barry.' What a noise! When they had finished, I blew out all the candles. 'No surprises so far,' I thought. The cake was delicious. 'Thanks, Sue,' I said. 'This is good.' 'Here's your present,' said Sue, giving me a small parcel. It was a pen. Mum and Dad gave me a nice watch and a new pullover. From Kevin I got a big book about football. 'Thank you, everybody,' I said. Still no surprises. Then the phone rang. 'That's your surprise, Barry,' said Dad. 'Go on, it's for you.' 'Hello,' I said. 'Barry Jones speaking.' 'Barry!' a voice boomed. 'Happy birthday! Uncle Tim here! From America! I want to invite you and your friend Kevin over for the summer. Do you want to come?'

activities.title: Read the Story: Barry's Birthday

content.passage:
It was May 22nd - my birthday!
'Happy birthday, dear,' said Mum when I got downstairs. 'The postman's just been. There are some cards for you. And there's a nice surprise.'
'What is it?' I asked.
'You'll find out tonight,' said Mum. 'At your party.'

On the bus to school, I tried to read my Chemistry book because Mr Law was giving us a test. But I couldn't think about Chemistry. I was thinking about my surprise. What could it be?
'What do you think it is?' I asked Kevin when I got to school.
'The Crown Jewels?' he suggested.
The bell went. The Chemistry test began. The Chemistry test finished. I had answered one question. I was still thinking about my surprise.

'I came top today,' said Sue when I got home. 'We had a test in Chemistry and I came top.'
I didn't say anything about my test.
'And I've made you a cake.'

At the party later, Sue brought the cake in with sixteen candles on it and everybody sang, 'Happy birthday, dear Barry.' What a noise! When they had finished, I blew out all the candles.
'No surprises so far,' I thought.

The cake was delicious. 'Thanks, Sue,' I said. 'This is good.'
'Here's your present,' said Sue, giving me a small parcel. It was a pen. Mum and Dad gave me a nice watch and a new pullover. From Kevin I got a big book about football.
'Thank you, everybody,' I said. Still no surprises. Then the phone rang.
'That's your surprise, Barry,' said Dad. 'Go on, it's for you.'
'Hello,' I said. 'Barry Jones speaking.'
'Barry!' a voice boomed. 'Happy birthday! Uncle Tim here! From America! I want to invite you and your friend Kevin over for the summer. Do you want to come?'

options.feedback: Incorrect. In an indirect question, the word order after the 'wh-' word is subject + verb, not verb + subject.

options.feedback: Incorrect. We don't use 'do/does/did' in the second part of an indirect question.

options.text: If I had enough money, I will buy a boat.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The main clause in the second conditional uses 'would' + infinitive, not 'will'.

options.text: If I had enough money, I would buy a boat.
options.feedback: Correct! This follows the structure: If + past simple, ... would + infinitive.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the second conditional?
questions.explanation: The second conditional is used for hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future. The structure is 'If + past simple, ... would + base verb'.

Correct! The past perfect 'had become' is used for an action that was completed before another action in the past.

questions.question: She (3) **has become** Queen on the 6th of February, 1952 when her father died.
questions.explanation: The past perfect tense ('had become') is used to describe an event that happened before another event in the past (the coronation).

options.feedback: This is a statement, not a question. It should end with a period or an exclamation mark to show excitement.
Correct! An exclamation mark shows the importance and excitement of the day.

questions.question: But this was her big day(4)**?**
questions.explanation: This is a declarative sentence expressing excitement, so an exclamation mark is the most appropriate punctuation.

options.feedback: This is a common spelling mistake.
Correct spelling!

questions.question: Kings and Queens from all over the (5) **werld** came to the ceremony.
questions.explanation: This is a spelling error. The correct spelling is 'world'.

options.feedback: The pronoun must agree with the noun 'Queen'.
Correct! 'Her' is the correct possessive pronoun for 'Queen'.

questions.question: Afterwards, the Queen, wearing (6) **his** crown, drove through London.
questions.explanation: The possessive pronoun must agree in gender with the noun it refers to. The Queen is female, so the pronoun is 'her'.

options.feedback: 'Spectacles' are glasses. The word for people watching an event is different.
Correct! 'Spectators' are people who watch an event.

questions.question: There were thousands of (7) **spectacles**.
questions.explanation: This is a vocabulary error. 'Spectacles' means eyeglasses. 'Spectators' are people who watch an event.

options.feedback: This action (waiting) happened before the main past event (the Queen driving by). We need the past perfect.
Correct! The past perfect 'had waited' shows the waiting happened before the main event in the past.

questions.question: Some (8) **have waited** in the streets for days to get a good place to watch.
questions.explanation: The past perfect tense ('had waited') is used because the waiting happened before the main past event (the parade).

options.feedback: The word 'every' is followed by a singular noun.
Correct! After 'every', we use a singular noun.

questions.question: There were parties in every town and every (9) **children** got a present.
questions.explanation: The determiner 'every' must be followed by a singular noun. The singular of 'children' is 'child'.

activities.title: Understanding Germs

content.passage: For centuries, people did not understand what caused diseases. It wasn't until the invention of the microscope that scientists could see the tiny world of microorganisms. These living things, also called organisms, are too small to be seen with the naked eye. Many of these organisms are harmless, but some, known as germs, can cause illness. Germs are found everywhere: in the air, on surfaces, and in our bodies. They can spread easily from person to person through coughing or touching contaminated surfaces. To protect ourselves, we can take simple but effective measures. For example, using a disinfectant to clean surfaces kills germs. Boiling water before drinking it is another crucial step to eliminate harmful organisms. Good personal hygiene, like washing hands frequently, is one of the best defenses against the spread of germs.

activities.title: A Drive in the Countryside

content.passage:
Last year, I spent my holiday in Wales, where the scenery is wonderful. One bright, sunny day, I decided to go for a drive. I drove out of town along the coast road. The sea was to my left about two kilometres away. Between the sea and the road was farmland. In one field there were a lot of cows with their heads down, grazing. In another field, close to me, a farmer on a tractor was ploughing. Behind the plough were lots of birds, looking for something to eat in the newly turned-over soil.

To the right of the road were some high, rocky hills. I turned off the main coast road and soon I was in a deep valley. Hills rose on both sides of the road. At first, the road climbed gently, but as I drove higher, it got steeper and steeper. Further up I could see a river to the left. I drove higher and higher and the river got narrower and narrower, until it was just a stream.

Near the top of the hill, the road ended. I got out of the car and climbed to the peak to look at the view of the valley below. At the end of the valley I could see the farmer on his tractor. Away in the distance I could just make out the sea. As I looked, I began to feel hungry and thirsty.

I went back down to the stream below. The water was cold and clear and tasted very good. I sat on a rock to eat my sandwiches, my back warmed by the sun. Suddenly a cloud came across the sun. I felt cold. A mist came down over the mountain. Soon I would not be able to see where I was going. I knew I had to leave. I put away a half-eaten sandwich, got into the car and drove back down the valley.

content.transcript: It isn’t easy to describe the man. He could have been anyone. He had straight, greyish hair. It was thin and quite long in places. I don’t think he went to a hairdresser’s very often. Perhaps he thought it wasn’t worth it as he didn’t have much hair lift. His eyes were tired - the eyes of a man who has seen a lot of sadness or worry. His face was tired too - tired and covered in lines. It wasn’t an ugly face, just a very very old one. He wore an old black jacket - not a sports jacket but the jacket from a long forgotten suit. Under the jacket was an open-necked shirt. His trousers, which didn’t match the jacket and looked too big for him, were a dull blue colour and full of holes. On his feet were a pair of battered shoes - not much good in the rain. ### The first thing you noticed about the man was his shoes. They were brightly polished and an unusual shape - long and pointed. Most people were wearing heavy shoes or boots, which made his stand out. Above the shoes, he was wearing a pair of light coloured trousers which made quite a contrast with the dark shoes. His jacket was the same colour as the shoes, very smart and beautifully cut. He had a white shirt and a flower pattern tie. His face was long and thin, and his short, pointed beard made it look even longer. His glasses caught the light as he moved his head from side to side quickly, like a bird, and his long dark hair swung from side to side.

content.transcript: Crossbreeding, or creating hybrid animals, is only possible when two animals are part of the same family. This is because their genetic makeup is similar enough to produce offspring. The liger, a mix of a male lion and a female tiger, is one famous example. Another is the cama, born from a male camel and a female llama. Scientists were interested in the cama because they hoped to combine the camel's size and strength with the llama's valuable wool coat. While these hybrids are fascinating, they often cannot reproduce themselves and usually live in captivity rather than in the wild.

activities.title: Reading: Rama - the Cama

content.passage:
Animals are divided into families. The house-cat is of the same family as its much bigger cousins, the lions of Africa and the tigers of India. The dog, the wolf and the jackal are part of the dog family. If animals are part of the same family, it is sometimes possible to crossbreed them to make a new animal. This was done several years ago when a lion was crossbred with a tiger, giving us a new animal called a ‘liger’. Now, it has been done again. The new animal is called a ‘cama’, and has been given the name Rama.

Rama the cama was born in Dubai in January, 1998. It is a cross between a male camel and a female llama. Although they are from the same family of animals, they are very different. Camels live mainly in hot countries like Arabia, whereas llamas live in mountainous parts of South America where it gets very, very cold. Because of the intense cold at heights of 4,000 metres, llamas have coats of long, heavy wool.

So what does Rama look like? Unlike its father, it has no hump on its back. Like its father, it has the short ears and the long tail of the camel. It is bigger than a llama but not as big as a camel. However, the wool coat of the llama, which is very valuable, unlike the hair coat of the camel, which has little value.

content.transcript: Many people debate whether city life is better than country life. The city is certainly more exciting than the countryside; however, it is also much noisier. In the city, you have many job opportunities. Unlike the countryside, where jobs can be limited, the city offers a wide range of careers. The cost of living is a major point of contrast. Whereas a large house in the country can be affordable, a small apartment in the city is often not as cheap. In terms of community, some say country life is better. Like my grandfather, many older people prefer the quiet and close-knit community. The air quality is also not the same. Although the city has parks, the air is generally not as clean as the fresh air in the country.

content.transcript: Welcome. Today we're looking at a classic landscape. In the distance, you can see a tall mountain range. From these mountains, a small stream begins its journey, growing into a wide river as it flows through the green valley below. content.transcript: Mike: Andy! Andy! Andy: Over here. Mike: There you are! I've been looking for you for hours! Are you Ok? Andy: Yes ... I'm fine. Mike: Are you hurt? Andy: I ... don't know. I'll try to get up. Aaah. No, I've hurt my leg. Mike: Here. Let me see. Mmm. I think it's broken. What happened? Andy: I was crossing the river when I slipped. I fell into the water and I must have hit my head on a rock, because I don't remember anything else until I heard you calling, just now. Mike: The river carried you miles. I'm surprised you didn't drown. Andy: I'm certainly very wet ... and very cold. Mike: Here, have my jacket. Andy: What time is it? Mike: Half past five. It's getting dark. We've got to get off this mountain before nightfall. Andy: So what are we going to do? You can't carry me down. Mike: That's true. You're too fat! Andy: Thanks a lot! Mike: I've got my mobile phone. I'll call for help. Andy: But ... do you know where we are? Mike: I think so. Let's look at the map. We came up this big valley together, and crossed the river once. Then we climbed this hill on the left - it's called High View - and you went on ahead towards Snow peak. Why didn't you wait for me? Andy: I wanted to see the view from the top. You were moaning about wanting to get back ... Mike: I was worried about the weather. Look, it's getting misty. It was sunny when we started ... Andy: Well, anyway. You must have fallen into this river here, on the west side of Snow peak. I waited for ages for you to come back, then I followed you up the top and saw the other river. I found your tracks on this side of the river, but nothing on the other side, so I followed the river down for about 5 kilometres. So I think we are about here, near Sheep Moor. Look! Those fields in the distance must be Cliff Farm. Andy: Ok. So call in the mountain rescue people. Mike: Right ... Oh, no! Andy: What? Mike: The battery on the phone's dead.

activities.title: A Drive in Wales

content.passage:
I decided to spend my holiday in Wales, and one day I went for a drive. I began on the main coast road. To my left, the sea stretched out to the horizon. In a large field, some cows were grazing peacefully. A bit closer to my car, a farmer on a red tractor was ploughing the newly-turned over soil, and a flock of birds followed him, looking for something to eat.

After a while, I turned off the coast road and headed inland. The road began to get higher and steeper. Soon, I could see a river in the valley below me. As I drove further up the mountain, the road became narrower, and the river also became narrower until it was just a small stream.

The road finally ended near the top of the hill. From there, I had to walk. The rocky peak was still high above me, but the view was already amazing. I could just make out the town where I was staying in the distance. After reaching the peak, I climbed down a little way because I was hungry and thirsty and wanted to eat my sandwiches.

The weather was hot and sunny as I started to eat. It was perfect. Suddenly, however, a cold mist rolled in from the sea. The clouds covered the sun, and it became quite cold. My perfect picnic was over!

sentences.original: There were lots of goats on top of the hill.

sentences.original: Some of the hills were to the right of the road.
sentences.explanation: The phrase 'To the right of the road' moves to the front for emphasis, and the verb 'were' is inverted with the subject 'some of the hills'.

sentences.original: A small, wooden boat was in the middle of the lake.

sentences.original: The Romans built a giant dam nearly 2,000 years ago.
sentences.explanation: The object 'a giant dam' becomes the subject. We use 'was built' (past simple passive) because the action happened in the past.
sentences.transformed: A giant dam was built by the Romans nearly 2,000 years ago.

sentences.original: The authorities will demolish the old castle.
sentences.explanation: The object 'the old castle' becomes the subject. We use 'will be demolished' (future simple passive). We can omit 'by the authorities' as it's obvious.
sentences.transformed: The old castle will be demolished.

sentences.original: A rescue team rescued two swimmers from the sea.
sentences.explanation: The object 'two swimmers' becomes the subject. We use 'were rescued' (past simple passive).
sentences.transformed: Two swimmers were rescued from the sea.

sentences.original: Bird-watchers have seen a black stork in this country.
sentences.explanation: The object 'a black stork' becomes the subject. We use 'has been seen' (present perfect passive) because the original sentence is in the present perfect.
sentences.transformed: A black stork has been seen in this country.

questions.question: Why does the witness think the accident happened?

content.transcript: Interviewer: Where were you exactly when the accident happened? Witness: I was in the baker's. I was buying a cake for my little daughter. It was her birthday. Interviewer: And you saw the accident. Witness: No. I heard the accident. There was a terrible crash and ran out of the shop. Interviewer: And what did you see? Witness: Two cars - a black one and a yellow one - had crashed into each other. Well, the yellow car had crashed into the black one. From behind. By the roundabout. Because of the fog, I suppose. You could hardly see your hand in front of your face. The two drivers were standing in the road, shouting at each other. And there was someone in the black car - hurt she was screaming. Then the police arrived - and the ambulance. Interviewer: Whose fault was it? Witness: The driver of the yellow car. I think. I think it was his fault. It looked as if he'd been driving too fast for the weather. But I don't know - I didn't see it, you see.

content.transcript: Interviewer: How do you feel now? Ed Shaw: Great. I nearly died, but I feel great now. Mrs Shaw: He felt awful. But he's better now. Interviewer: How long were you in hospital? Mrs Shaw: He was in there nearly a whole week. And the nurses were wonderful. Ed Shaw: Honey, it was four days. Not a week. Mrs Shaw: Well, four days, then. A long time, anyway. Interviewer: And what happened exactly? Ed Shaw: In the hospital? Interviewer: Er, no. What happened when you collapsed? Mrs Shaw: I told him to wear a hat. Just that morning I'd said; Honey, don't forget your hat. It's gonna be hot today; And what did he say? 'It never gets hot in England. This isn't California; And what happens? He falls ... Ed Shaw: Honey, can you let me explain? We went for a walk in the hills - those hills over there - and it was fine. Ok, the sun was shining, but there was a slight breeze - a very pleasant gentle wind - and it didn't feel hot. Mrs Shaw: But then we stopped at a restaurant and where did he want to sit? Outside! Outside in the sun. He knows he can't stand the heat and where does he want to sit? Outside. Ed Shaw: Honey! Please. We stopped for lunch and, yes, we sat outside in the garden of this restaurant - it was her idea - and there was ... Mrs Shaw: It was NOT! You said ... Ed Shaw: Anyway, we sat in the garden, and there was no wind, and the sun got hotter, and I didn't notice, and the next thing I knew I was in hospital. Mrs Shaw: He just collapsed. Right in the middle of lunch. He didn't even finish it. I just telling him that he was looking a bit strange when he just closed his eyes and fell off the chair. Well, I tell you, I was worried. He'd never done that before. But the people in the restaurant were marvellous. They called the ambulance and two hours Later we were in the hospital. He'd had a small heart attack. The doctor said ... Ed Shaw: The doctor said I was Ok but just needed a rest and some peace and quiet. Peace and quiet - fat chance!

content.transcript:
Don: I had a dream last night. Well, a nightmare, actually.
Jim: Really? What about?
Don: It was awful. I was terrified. There were men with horrible faces and...
Jim: Just a minute. Calm down. Begin at the beginning. Now ... Where were you?
Don: I dreamt that we were working in the fields and ...
Jim: Who was? Who were you with?
Don: My brother. My elder brother. We were planting seed for next year. And I was driving the tractor. And it was brilliant weather. Then suddenly ...
Jim: Slow down. Slow down. What happened?
Don: I heard somebody shouting. Then I saw two men running towards us.
Jim: Who were they?
Don: I don't know. But they were really scary. One was holding a gun. My brother and I wanted to run but we couldn't move. It was terrible.
Jim: So how did you escape?
Don: I woke up.

options.feedback: Correct. We use 'is to be' to talk about future plans, often in a formal or official context.

sentences.text: At the wedding, the men ___ (dance) outside when it ___ (start) to rain.

options.feedback: This is the literal meaning, not the metaphorical one.

The word 'flooded' here refers to quantity, not quality.

questions.explanation: To be 'flooded' with something means to receive so much of it that it's difficult to manage.

options.feedback: While the news might be sad, the metaphor refers to how it spread.

options.text: The news was about a fire.
options.feedback: The fire is used as a comparison for speed.
Excellent! Forest fires spread very rapidly, so this means the news traveled fast.
This metaphor doesn't comment on the truth of the news.

questions.question: What does 'like a forest fire' mean in the sentence 'The news of the Princess's death spread around the country _like a forest fire_.'?
questions.explanation: The phrase 'like a forest fire' is a simile used to describe something that spreads very quickly and is hard to control.

options.feedback: A hurricane is the opposite of quiet and slow.

activities.title: Present Perfect vs. Past Simple

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: Over the years there ___ (to be) many disastrous volcanic eruptions.
sentences.explanation: We use the Present Perfect ('have been') because 'Over the years' indicates a period of time that continues up to the present.

sentences.text: The worst ___ (to take place) in Krakatoa in 1883.
sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('took place') because a specific past time ('in 1883') is mentioned.

sentences.text: Over 36,000 people ___ (to lose) their lives.
sentences.explanation: This event is part of the 1883 eruption, so we use the Past Simple ('lost').

sentences.text: A large passenger plane ___ (to crash) in the mountains.
sentences.explanation: We use the Present Perfect ('has crashed') to describe a recent event with a present result (the plane is still crashed, rescue is ongoing).

sentences.text: So far rescue teams ___ (to find) no survivors.
sentences.explanation: The phrase 'So far' indicates a period up to the present, so we use the Present Perfect ('have found').

sentences.text: The plane ___ (to take off) from London two days ago.
sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('took off') because a specific past time ('two days ago') is mentioned.

sentences.text: The pilot ___ (to contact) Jeddah airport one hour before the plane crashed.
sentences.explanation: This action happened at a specific time before another past event, so we use the Past Simple ('contacted').

sentences.text: Several people ___ (to die) recently as a result of traffic accidents.
sentences.explanation: 'Recently' often signals the use of the Present Perfect ('have died') for recent past events with present relevance.

sentences.text: Last Thursday two small children ___ (to be) killed by a speeding car.
sentences.explanation: We use the Past Simple ('were') because a specific past time ('Last Thursday') is mentioned.

activities.title: Combining Sentences with Relative Clauses

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The bus has had an accident. I come to school on it.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with necessary information, so the preposition 'on' goes at the end of the clause. No commas are needed.
correct_answers: The bus I come to school on has had an accident.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The Great Fire of London happened in 1666. Thousands of buildings were destroyed in it.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with additional information. The preposition 'in' moves to the beginning of the clause with 'which'. The clause is placed between commas.
correct_answers: The Great Fire of London, in which thousands of buildings were destroyed, happened in 1666.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The man has mysteriously disappeared. I was talking to him yesterday.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with necessary information. The preposition 'to' goes at the end of the clause. No commas are needed.
correct_answers: The man I was talking to yesterday has mysteriously disappeared.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The Armenian earthquake killed over 25,000 people. I have to write about it in the next lesson.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with additional information. The preposition 'about' moves to the beginning of the clause with 'which'. The clause is placed between commas.
correct_answers: The Armenian earthquake, about which I have to write in the next lesson, killed over 25,000 people.

prompts.prompt: Combine these sentences: The flood of 1953 is still the worst in living memory for the people of The Netherlands. New dams were built after it.
prompts.explanation: This is a relative clause with additional information. The preposition 'after' moves to the beginning of the clause with 'which'. The clause is placed between commas.
correct_answers: The flood of 1953, after which new dams were built, is still the worst in living memory for the people of The Netherlands.

activities.compensates: This activity provides interactive practice for the concepts in Pupil's Book page 15, section 3, and is based on Workbook Activity B.
activities.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using a relative clause. Remember to place the preposition correctly.

activities.title: Reading: The Eruption of Krakatoa

content.passage: History has recorded many disastrous volcanic eruptions, but few have been as powerful as the one that occurred in Krakatoa. The eruption, which took place in 1883, was one of the most violent volcanic events in modern history. The explosion was so loud that people heard it nearly 5,000 kilometers away. For months after the event, strange weather patterns affected the entire globe. The eruption and the tsunamis it created caused immense destruction. In the immediate aftermath, over 36,000 people lost their lives. The island of Krakatoa, in which the volcano was located, almost completely disappeared. Scientists today continue to study the event to better understand volcanic activity. The area, to which researchers now travel frequently, has become a living laboratory for studying how life recolonizes a devastated landscape.

content.instruction: Arrange the news reports in the correct order based on the time they were released.
correctOrder: 13.00: Flash. Earthquake in Armenia. The town of Spivak at 11.41 local time. 6.9 on the Richter scale. First reports say that damage is serious.

14.00: Armenia: Considerable loss of life reported. 'The buildings were very badly built,' said an eye-witness. 'They fell down like packs of cards.' The rescue workers have no equipment and are working with their bare hands.

15.00: Armenia: Spivak completely flattened. Most of population - 20,000 - killed. In Leninakan, Armenia's largest city, thousands of people are homeless. One in five of buildings destroyed. 'We urgently need tents and blankets,' a spokesman said.

16.00: Earthquake Epidemic Risk: Rescue workers say there is a danger of cholera and typhoid following the Armenian earthquake. 'There is no clean drinking water,' said a nurse. 'Disease can spread very quickly. We need clean water now.'
17.00: Earthquake: The Armenian earthquake is the strongest since 1964 when an earthquake measuring 8.6 on the Richter scale hit Alaska.
23.00: President to return: President Gorbachov is interrupting his trip to the USA to take charge of rescue efforts. Officials number of dead 55,000. Some say this could reach 100,000.

activities.title: Reporting the News

sentences.original: 'We urgently need tents and blankets,' a spokesman said.
sentences.explanation: In reported speech, 'we' changes to 'they' and the present tense 'need' changes to the past tense 'needed'.
sentences.transformed: A spokesman said that they urgently needed tents and blankets.

sentences.original: 'The buildings were very badly built,' said an eye-witness.
sentences.explanation: The past simple 'were' changes to the past perfect 'had been' in reported speech.
sentences.transformed: An eye-witness said that the buildings had been very badly built.

sentences.original: 'There is no clean drinking water,' said a nurse.
sentences.explanation: The present tense 'is' changes to the past tense 'was' in reported speech.
sentences.transformed: A nurse said that there was no clean drinking water.

sentences.original: 'Disease can spread very quickly,' she added.
sentences.explanation: The modal verb 'can' changes to 'could' in reported speech.
sentences.transformed: She added that disease could spread very quickly.

content.transcript:
Receptionist: City TV, how can I help you? 
Student: Hello, I'm calling about the Work Experience Opportunity, WEO 5, that I saw advertised. 
Receptionist: Yes, of course. We have several vacancies for students interested in media. Are you in your last year at school? 
Student: Yes, I am. The notice mentioned an excellent salary for a permanent position. Does the work experience offer payment? 
Receptionist: The work experience itself is unpaid, but it's a great way to see if you enjoy working in news, theatre, or music production. Many of our work experience students go on to get permanent positions with us. 
Student: That sounds interesting. What should I do next? 
Receptionist: You'll need to send us your CV and a cover letter explaining why you're interested in this opportunity. You can find the email address on our website.

activities.title: Worthwhile Jobs

questions.question: Which person says, 'I help to build the future of the country.'?
Which person says, 'We also save people's houses and their places of work.'?
Which person says, 'People think we just make money for ourselves.'?
Which person says, 'We work very long hours and they don't pay us much.'?

content.transcript: Presenter: Listen to the four interviews and match the statements. Reporter: Mrs Ibrahim, do you think your job is worthwhile? Mrs Ibrahim: Of course being a teacher is a worthwhile job. I share what I know with my students. Every day they learn a little more from me. And I help to prepare them for life after school. So my job is definitely worthwhile. I help to build the future of the country. Reporter: Mary, is your job worthwhile? Mary: Of course it's a worthwhile job. We save lives. We also save people's houses and their places of work. We often have to go to a factory to put out a fire. Factories are dangerous places. But the most important part of my work is teaching people about fire prevention, about how to make sure fires don't start. Reporter: Mr Habib, do you do a worthwhile job? Mr Habib: I enjoy being a businessman. And I think it's a valuable job. People think we just make money for ourselves, but that's not true. We business people also make a lot of money for the country. We create the money to pay for nurses and teachers and firefighters. And we create jobs for other people. Reporter: And finally, Miss Ahmed, I'm sure your job is worthwhile. Miss Ahmed: Well, I'm a hospital nurse. And people don't seem to think this is a very worthwhile job. We work very long hours and they don't pay us much. But I enjoy my work. I take care of people who are ill and help them get better. I most enjoy looking after children. It makes me very happy to see a sick child get well. Yes, I do think my job is worthwhile.

activities.title: Meet the Students

content.passage:
Patrick's ambition after leaving school is to become a doctor. However, he is not very good at Chemistry or Biology. His best subject is Mathematics. For the last year he has been going to evening classes in first-aid. He is adventurous and when he can, he goes underwater swimming.

Diana is very efficient and likes organizing things. Since the beginning of the year she has been planning all the class trips and outings. She writes all the letters and notices on her computer. Her best subject is English, but she enjoys Mathematics more. At the weekend she goes sailing and she is the secretary of the local sailing club. She would like to go into Government Administration.

Andrew is not very good at any subjects at school although he will probably pass his final examinations. He has a driving licence and every weekend he drives out into the country and then walks for hours. He is very interested in nature and has been reading about trees, plants and flowers for almost two years. He would like to work in the country. He is very hard-working and gets on well with people.

Justin has two very different hobbies: driving his father's new car in the country, and cooking. He spends most Saturdays driving along muddy roads. On Sundays he cooks all the meals for the whole family. He has been doing this since he was 12. His best subjects are Mathematics and Sport. Both his parents are teachers, but he would like to go into business.

Clare has been collecting folk-music CDs for three years. She now has 150. She has lots of friends and she likes playing her music to them. One day she would like to sing or play on television. At school her best subjects are History and Music. She has a good speaking voice and often acts in the plays put on by the school drama group.

Fareeda is a very helpful young woman and is very good at helping others in her class. She has been driving for six months and at the weekend she takes her disabled young sister in her parents' car. At school she is excellent at History, but she does not want to go to college. She wants to help other people in some way, perhaps as social worker.

activities.title: Grammar Rules Check

statements.statement: The Present Perfect Continuous emphasizes how long an action has been going on.
statements.explanation: Correct. The continuous form focuses on the duration of the action.

statements.statement: The Present Perfect Simple is used for actions that have been happening very recently.
statements.explanation: Incorrect. The continuous tense usually refers to recent actions. The simple tense can refer to actions from a long time ago.

statements.statement: Verbs like 'know', 'believe', and 'need' are commonly used in the continuous tense.
statements.explanation: Incorrect. These are stative verbs and are not usually used with the continuous tense.

statements.statement: We use the Present Perfect Continuous to talk about the present effects of a recent, continuous action.
statements.explanation: Correct. For example: 'It has been raining, so the ground is wet.'

statements.statement: After 'would like' or 'would prefer', you must use the -ing form of the verb.
statements.explanation: Incorrect. After 'would like/love/prefer/hate', you must use the 'to + infinitive' form.

activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led review of grammar rules and comprehension questions.
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the statements about the Present Perfect tenses from Pupil's Book page 20. Decide if they are true or false.

activities.title: Verb + Infinitive or -ing?

options.feedback: Incorrect. After 'would like' and 'would prefer', we use the infinitive.
Correct. The structure is 'would like/prefer + to + infinitive'.

options.feedback: While this is grammatically possible, the other option is also correct.
While this is grammatically possible, the other option is also correct.

options.text: Both 'to work / to work' and 'working / working' are correct.
options.feedback: Correct! The verbs 'hate' and 'start' can be followed by either the infinitive or the -ing form with little change in meaning.

options.feedback: Check the rules for 'would hate' and 'start'.

options.text: to be / to look or looking
options.feedback: Correct! After 'would hate' we must use 'to + infinitive'. After 'start', both forms are possible.

options.feedback: Correct. 'Never' with a life experience uses the simple form.
Incorrect. The continuous form is not used with 'never' in this context.

questions.question: She ______ India in her life.

options.feedback: This implies the homework is finished, but the context suggests an ongoing excuse.
Correct. This explains the reason for not tidying the room; it's an ongoing action.

questions.question: Why haven't you tidied your room? I ______ my homework.

options.feedback: Correct. 'Know' is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous form.
Incorrect. 'Know' is a stative verb.

questions.question: We ______ him for a long time.

options.feedback: Correct. 'Arrive' is a short action, not a continuous one.
Incorrect. 'Arrive' describes a moment in time, not a duration.

questions.question: Why ______ yet?

options.feedback: This doesn't emphasize the repeated, recent nature of the action as well as the continuous form.

options.feedback: This focuses on completion, but the sentence emphasizes the duration.

content.transcript: For the new project manager position, we are looking for a very specific set of qualities. First, the successful candidate must show great diligence; we need someone who is thorough and persistent. They also need to be confident in their decisions. options.text: Must be able to use a computer and speak a foreign language

questions.question: What is a key requirement for the job at the Sunrise Travel Agency?
Which job requires the applicant to be ready to work abroad in Europe or the USA?
What is the contact method for the job at the zoo?
Which organization is looking for both men and women to join them?

content.transcript:
Speaker 1: Would you like to work abroad? Would you like to help people in poorer countries? The World Aid Organization is looking for young people to help in the following areas. Education: we need young men and women to help with teaching reading and writing to children at Primary Schools. Health: we need young people who want to get experience of work in clinics. You must be in good health, under 20 years old and be ready to live abroad for at least 6 months. Send for an application form to P.O. Box 791.
Speaker 2: The famous Gate Restaurant is right in the centre of town. We are looking for people to train as cooks. We serve food from all over the world, so this is a wonderful opportunity for a young man who wants to start a career in the restaurant business. Come and see us for an interview. Ring 35692 and make an appointment.
Speaker 3: We know that many of you have booked your holidays at the Sunrise Travel Agency. And now we have a vacancy for a clerk. It will be your job to sell holidays and travel tickets to the public. You must be able to use a computer and speak at least one foreign language. Both men and women may apply. Write to P.O. Box 3815, giving details of yourself, and enclose a photograph. This could be the start of a very rewarding career.
Speaker 4: The Television Company is looking for a young man or woman to train as a reporter and presenter of news programmes. After training in this country, the successful applicant must be ready to work abroad in Europe or the United States for at least three months. He or she must have a good speaking voice, be interested in news and politics, and speak English fluently. Telephone 9582 for more details and an application form.
Speaker 5: Do you like working with animals? Are you interested in the environment? Are you interested in saving rare animals? There is a vacancy at the zoo for a trainee zookeeper. You must be male, healthy and ready to work hard. Write to P.O. Box 1269 for more details.
Speaker 6: We fight crime. We make sure that people drive safely. We help and protect people. We offer a long, secure and rewarding career to men and women. Who are we? The Police. Come and join us. Ring 4186 and find out more.

activities.title: Using Connectors Correctly

options.feedback: Correct! 'As a result' shows the consequence of his laziness and lack of language skills.
Incorrect. 'In addition' is used to add more information, not to show a result.
Incorrect. 'As well as' is used within a sentence to add another item, not to link two separate ideas of cause and effect.

questions.question: He was lazy and could not speak a foreign language. ______, he was not given the job.
questions.explanation: The second sentence is a direct consequence of the first. Therefore, a connector of consequence like 'As a result', 'Therefore', or 'Consequently' is needed.

options.feedback: Incorrect. 'Therefore' shows a result. Being conscientious is an additional positive quality, not a result of being polite.
Correct! 'Furthermore' is used to add another piece of information to support a point.
Incorrect. 'Because' explains a reason, it doesn't add a new, related point.

questions.question: She is polite and friendly. ______, she is very conscientious.
questions.explanation: 'Furthermore' and 'In addition' are used at the beginning of a sentence to add a new, related point.

options.feedback: Correct! 'That is why' clearly connects the reason (good marks) with the result (wanting to be a doctor).
Incorrect. 'Also' adds information, but doesn't show the strong cause-and-effect link needed here.
Incorrect. This connector adds another point, it doesn't explain the consequence.

questions.question: Mahmoud always got good marks in Science. ______ he wanted to become a doctor.
questions.explanation: This sentence structure requires a phrase that shows consequence. 'That is why', 'Therefore', and 'So' are all good options.

options.feedback: Incorrect. This shows a result, but the gloves are just another item of clothing he wore.
Correct! 'As well as' is used to add another item to a list within a sentence.
Incorrect. This shows a consequence, not an addition to a list.

questions.question: He wore a hat and a coat ______ woollen gloves.
questions.explanation: To add items within a sentence, we can use connectors like 'and', 'as well as', or 'together with'.

content.passage:
Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing to **apply for** the position of Junior Marketing Assistant, as advertised on your website. I have recently graduated with a degree in Business Administration and have over a year of **experience of** working in a busy office environment during an internship.

I am particularly **interested in** this role because your company is a leader in sustainable technology. **Furthermore**, my university studies included several modules on digital marketing. **As a result**, I am proficient with all major social media platforms and analytics tools. I am a hard-working and dedicated individual. **In addition**, I am a quick learner and work well in a team. 

I believe I have the necessary skills and enthusiasm for this job. I would be **grateful for** the **chance of** an interview to discuss my application further. I **look forward to** hearing from you.

Sincerely,

Ahmad Saleh

activities.title: How to Make Fish Curry

content.passage:
**James:** What are you doing, mum?
**Mother:** I'm making a fish curry.
**James:** That sounds good. And these are the ingredients?
**Mother:** Yes, I always prepare them before I start cooking.
**James:** So... that's the fish ... and the tomatoes and onions ... and that's garlic, isn't it?
**Mother:** Yes. Two peeled and chopped tomatoes, two chopped onions, and three crushed cloves of garlic.
**James:** What's that round, brown thing?
**Mother:** It's a *loomi* - a small, dried lime.
**James:** And those other things... they're spices, I suppose.
**Mother:** Yes, two teaspoons of *babsar* - that's a mixture of spices. And ... half a teaspoon of turmeric, half a teaspoon of chilli powder and a quarter of a teaspoon of ground ginger.
**James:** What's in this bowl?
**Mother:** Lemon juice ... about one teaspoon.
**James:** Anything else?
**Mother:** Oil for frying, and, of course, salt and pepper.
**James:** So those are the ingredients. How do you actually cook the curry, then?
**Mother:** First you fry the onions and garlic. Then you add the spices and fry for a further two minutes. Next you add the tomatoes, *loomi*, lemon juice, salt and pepper. After that, you cover the mixture with water and simmer for fifteen minutes.
**James:** What about the fish?
**Mother:** While the mixture is boiling gently, you fry the pieces of fish.
**James:** How long for?
**Mother:** Until they are golden brown. Then you put the fish into the sauce and simmer for a further fifteen minutes... and that's it... fish curry.
**James:** Simple, isn't it?
